name: Madrid
peak_smog_season: Summer photochemical ozone & winter thermal inversion

analogue_current.note: Shares an equivalent Csa seasonal temperature and rainfall cycle.

analogue_2050.note: Hot semi-arid conditions with prolonged summer heatwaves >40°C.

urban_fact: A ring-and-radial street system surrounds a dense centre set on Spain’s elevated central plateau.
educational_debrief: Madrid's location on Spain's dry central plateau, the meseta, far from any navigable river or coast, was chosen more for its central position on the peninsula than for any natural advantage of terrain or water — a rare case among European capitals. Its ring-and-radial street pattern shows centuries of growth outward from a single royal center, most recently the M-30 and M-40 ring roads that now encircle a metropolitan area far larger than the historic core. Hot, dry Mediterranean summers combined with that inland, riverless setting make the city's mountain-reservoir water supply an unusually exposed resource for a European capital of its size.
cryptic_clue: A stone slab in a crowded plaza marks the zero point from which every road on the peninsula radiates. Fitting, since no capital in Western Europe sits higher above sea level.
image_caption: Historic Plaza Mayor in central Madrid, Spain

name: Barcelona
peak_smog_season: Spring Saharan dust intrusions & summer port emissions

analogue_current.note: Mediterranean coastal climate with mild winters.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, drier Mediterranean climate regime.

urban_fact: The Eixample’s chamfered grid sits between the Mediterranean coast and the Collserola hills.
educational_debrief: Barcelona's grid-like Eixample district, with its distinctive chamfered street corners, was the deliberate design of 19th-century engineer Ildefons Cerdà, who angled the corners to improve sightlines, ventilation, and space for the streetcars and traffic of his day — a plan built to expand beyond the cramped medieval old town rather than replace it. For much of the 20th century the city's industrial waterfront cut it off from its own beaches; hosting the 1992 Summer Olympics gave Barcelona the occasion to demolish that industrial shoreline and reorient the city back toward the Mediterranean it sits on. Wedged between the sea and the Collserola hills, the city has limited room to expand outward, which is part of why it is one of the densest urban areas in Western Europe.
cryptic_clue: A basilica begun in the 1880s has never stopped rising — one architect's death, a civil war, and well over a century later, it's still ringed by cranes.
image_caption: Aerial view of La Sagrada Família and the Torre Glòries in Barcelona

name: London
peak_smog_season: Winter particulate spikes & summer ozone episodes

analogue_current.note: Maritime North Sea temperate climate.

analogue_2050.note: Shifts toward warmer Mediterranean-like summers.

urban_fact: A polycentric metropolis grew around the Thames, layered rail networks, and former village centres.
educational_debrief: London grew not as a single planned city but as a patchwork of once-separate villages and market towns that fused together along the Thames as rail and Underground lines linked them, which is why it still reads as a polycentric city of local high streets rather than one dense core. The Thames Barrier, completed downstream of the city center in the 1980s, exists precisely because a tidal river running through a low-lying basin leaves central London exposed to storm surge pushed in from the North Sea. That same river gave the city its reason for being in the first place: Roman Londinium was founded where the Thames could still be bridged but remained deep enough for seagoing ships.
cryptic_clue: Legend holds that if the ravens ever leave the riverside fortress on its eastern edge, the kingdom falls. So for centuries, someone has kept their wings clipped.
image_caption: Palace of Westminster and River Thames in London, UK

name: Paris
peak_smog_season: Spring agricultural ammonia & summer traffic ozone

analogue_current.note: Temperate oceanic Western European basin.

analogue_2050.note: Warm temperate climate with significantly hotter summer peaks.

urban_fact: A compact core shaped by boulevards is encircled by the périphérique and a much larger regional rail city.
educational_debrief: Paris's dense, uniform street wall of cream-colored stone buildings dates largely to a single sweeping 19th-century renovation ordered by Napoleon III and carried out by Baron Haussmann, who cut wide boulevards through the old medieval street pattern to improve traffic flow, sanitation, and sightlines. That historic core is now ringed by the Boulevard Périphérique, a ring road built along the path of the city's demolished 19th-century fortifications, beyond which a much larger and far less dense metropolitan region continues to grow. Because the boundaries of Paris proper have barely changed since Haussmann's era, the city remains unusually compact and dense compared with its sprawling wider region.
cryptic_clue: An iron tower thrown up for a single World's Fair was meant to come down after twenty years. Instead it became the skyline's signature and one of the most-visited monuments on Earth.
image_caption: Haussmannian urban fabric and Eiffel Tower over the Seine, Paris

name: Berlin
peak_smog_season: Winter domestic heating & continental transport smog

analogue_current.note: Central European transitional maritime-continental.

analogue_2050.note: Warm temperate climate with drier summer periods.

urban_fact: Multiple historic centres, lakes, waterways, and extensive green space give the city a dispersed form.
educational_debrief: Berlin's dispersed, multi-centered layout owes much to its 20th-century history: the city was split into occupation sectors after World War II and then physically divided by the Berlin Wall for nearly three decades, forcing East and West Berlin to each develop their own downtown, transit network, and infrastructure that the reunified city has spent decades stitching back together. The surrounding landscape of lakes, rivers, and forests is a legacy of the last Ice Age, whose retreating glaciers carved the flat, water-rich terrain of the North German Plain the city sits on. That abundance of surface water is part of why, despite a temperate oceanic climate, Berlin's water utility already flags long-term supply as a growing concern amid rising demand and drier summers.
cryptic_clue: For 28 years, one street could put you in two different worlds. Then one night in 1989, crowds took hammers to the concrete seam between them.
image_caption: Brandenburg Gate at Pariser Platz in Berlin, Germany

name: Rome
peak_smog_season: Summer ozone & winter valley vehicle exhaust

analogue_current.note: Mediterranean basin climate with hot dry summers.

analogue_2050.note: Eastern Mediterranean hot subtropical conditions.

urban_fact: Ancient routes and later ring roads structure a low-rise metropolis around the Tiber.
educational_debrief: Rome's skyline stays famously low-rise in large part because of strict height and zoning limits, and because any major excavation risks running into archaeological remains — a practical constraint from building continuously on the same site for roughly 2,800 years. The city still draws on many of the same spring-fed sources its ancient aqueducts once tapped, including the restored Acqua Vergine that still feeds the Trevi Fountain today, and a Mediterranean climate of hot, increasingly dry summers is expected to put growing pressure on that historic water supply. Modern Rome's ring roads and radial arteries largely follow the lines of ancient Roman roads that once radiated out from the city to every corner of the empire, a layout that has shaped the region's transport network for two millennia.
cryptic_clue: Legend has twin brothers, raised by a she-wolf, founding a city on seven hills. Toss a coin over your shoulder into a fountain here and, they say, you're bound to return.
image_caption: The Flavian Amphitheatre (Colosseum) in central Rome, Italy

name: Tokyo
peak_smog_season: Summer high humidity and photochemical ozone

analogue_current.note: Pacific coast Japanese humid subtropical.

analogue_2050.note: Humid subtropical with intensified summer heat and rainfall.

urban_fact: An immense rail-oriented urban region wraps around Tokyo Bay with many strong subcentres.
educational_debrief: Tokyo's sprawling, rail-oriented form comes from a development pattern in which private railway companies built lines out toward the edges of the Kanto Plain and then developed the land and department stores around their own stations, producing a metropolis organized around dozens of dense rail hubs rather than one downtown. The city took its current name and role only when the site of the shogunate's Edo Castle became the emperor's seat in the 19th century, displacing the older imperial capital of Kyoto. Much of central and eastern Tokyo sits on low-lying land reclaimed from Tokyo Bay and river deltas, which is a key reason the city and national government invest so heavily in flood and storm-surge infrastructure.
cryptic_clue: Renamed 'Eastern Capital' when the emperor moved in, this city's best-known intersection can flood with thousands of pedestrians every time the lights change.
image_caption: Shinjuku high-density skyscraper cluster in Tokyo, Japan

name: Seoul
peak_smog_season: Spring yellow dust & winter transboundary particulates

analogue_current.note: Korean peninsula monsoon regime.

analogue_2050.note: Subtropical shift with warmer winters and heavier summer monsoon.

urban_fact: Dense districts occupy the Han River basin, constrained and divided by steep wooded mountains.
educational_debrief: Seoul's rapid transformation from a war-damaged city in the 1950s into one of the world's largest metropolitan economies is often called, in Korea, the 'Miracle on the Han River' — a period of concentrated industrial growth and dense apartment-block construction that gave the city its now-familiar skyline of high-rise housing towers. The surrounding terrain of steep, forested mountains leaves relatively little flat, buildable land within the Han River basin, which is part of why the city grew so vertically rather than sprawling outward like many other capitals of similar population. Seoul's location only tens of kilometers south of the heavily fortified Demilitarized Zone dividing the Korean Peninsula has also long shaped its urban planning and infrastructure around the reality of that nearby border.
cryptic_clue: Its own name simply means 'capital' in the local tongue — the only one of its kind with no other meaning behind it. A viral song about one of its glossier districts was the first video ever to cross a billion views.
image_caption: Skyline view from Namsan over central Seoul, South Korea

name: Beijing
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating inversion & spring Gobi sandstorms

analogue_current.note: North China Plain monsoon continental.

analogue_2050.note: Semi-arid warming with hotter summer extremes.

urban_fact: Concentric ring roads extend from an historic north–south axis across a broad inland plain.
educational_debrief: Beijing's urban plan still follows a strict north–south axis inherited from imperial-era cosmology, which held that the emperor's throne should align with the pole star; that axis, running through the old Forbidden City, has been extended in modern times by new administrative and Olympic districts built along the same line. Sitting on a dry inland plain far from any major river, the city has long struggled to supply water to its enormous population, a shortage severe enough that China built a system of long-distance canals and tunnels to pipe water north from the Yangtze basin. Beijing's position near the edge of the Gobi and Mongolian steppe also exposes it to seasonal dust storms, a challenge distinct from — but sometimes compounding — its more chronic urban air-pollution problems.
cryptic_clue: Its name translates to 'Northern Capital.' At its center sits a moated, walled palace complex so vast, and once so restricted, that emperors called it forbidden for five centuries.
image_caption: Beijing CBD skyline with CITIC Tower, viewed from the southeast

name: Shanghai
peak_smog_season: Winter regional haze & summer high-humidity ozone

analogue_current.note: Yangtze River Delta subtropical marine.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter tropical-trending summers and typhoons.

urban_fact: A dense river-and-port metropolis spreads across the flat Yangtze delta around the Huangpu River.
educational_debrief: Shanghai's waterfront Bund, lined with early-20th-century European-style banks and trading houses, is a physical remnant of the era when the city operated as a treaty port carved into foreign concessions rather than a single unified Chinese city — a split administrative history that shaped its early street patterns near the historic core. Built on the soft, waterlogged sediment of the Yangtze delta, the city has experienced significant land subsidence from decades of groundwater pumping and construction pressure, compounding its already high exposure to flooding on famously flat, low-lying terrain. That combination of low elevation, delta location, and dense construction is why Shanghai now relies on an extensive network of levees, floodgates, and storm-surge defenses along the Huangpu River to protect the city center.
cryptic_clue: Its name simply means 'upon the sea.' A row of colonial-era banks along the waterfront now stares across the river at a forest of towers that didn't exist forty years ago.
image_caption: Pudong skyline and waterfront viewed from the Bund, Shanghai, China

name: Hong Kong
peak_smog_season: Autumn/winter Pearl River Delta regional smog

analogue_current.note: South China monsoon subtropical.

analogue_2050.note: Tropical monsoonal temperatures year-round.

urban_fact: Very dense urban districts are compressed between steep mountains, islands, and Victoria Harbour.
educational_debrief: Hong Kong's extreme vertical density is largely a function of geography: with steep mountainsides covering most of its land area, only a narrow fringe around Victoria Harbour was ever easily buildable, pushing the city to build upward rather than outward and to reclaim large amounts of new land directly from the harbour itself. The territory's return to China in 1997 followed the expiry of a 99-year lease Britain had held over the New Territories, the rural hinterland that makes up most of Hong Kong's land area beyond the dense urban core on Hong Kong Island and Kowloon. Because so much of the population is concentrated on reclaimed, low-lying harbourfront land, the city remains exposed to storm surge from the typhoons that regularly track through the South China Sea each summer and autumn.
cryptic_clue: Its name translates to 'Fragrant Harbour.' A former colony returned to its mainland neighbor in 1997, its skyline now climbs a steep peak served by a century-old funicular.
image_caption: Central skyline and IFC building seen from the Star Ferry crossing Victoria Harbour, Hong Kong

name: Singapore
peak_smog_season: Late summer episodic transboundary peat fire haze

analogue_current.note: Equatorial humid tropical rainforest.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified equatorial heat and extreme humidity.

urban_fact: A planned island city combines high-density transit corridors, reservoirs, and a major global port.
educational_debrief: Despite sitting in a wet tropical climate, Singapore has long faced real water insecurity because its small land area leaves little room for reservoirs, and for decades the city depended heavily on imported water from Malaysia under long-standing bilateral agreements. In response, Singapore built out a strategy — officially described as its 'Four National Taps' — that combines local catchment, imported water, reclaimed wastewater, and desalination to reduce that historic dependency. The city-state has also physically grown through extensive land reclamation, expanding its territory well beyond its original coastline, a process closely tied to its role as one of the world's busiest shipping ports at the narrow, strategic chokepoint of the Strait of Malacca.
cryptic_clue: Its name means 'Lion City' in an old Sanskrit-derived tongue — though the beast guarding its harbourfront comes spliced with a fish's tail instead.
image_caption: Central Business District skyline viewed from the Lower Boardwalk of Marina Bay, Singapore

name: Mumbai
peak_smog_season: Winter post-monsoon thermal inversion and construction dust

analogue_current.note: Konkan coast intense southwest monsoon.

analogue_2050.note: Heavy tropical monsoons with extreme pre-monsoon heat.

urban_fact: The metropolis occupies a narrow coastal peninsula and islands, creating a strongly linear north–south form.
educational_debrief: Mumbai began as an archipelago of seven marshy islands that the British East India Company gradually joined through centuries of land reclamation, which is why the metropolis today reads as a long, narrow spine running north from the historic port rather than a compact, circular city. That reclaimed, low-lying geography leaves large parts of the city just above sea level, and the annual monsoon regularly floods the streets and rail lines its dense population depends on for its daily commute. Mumbai's role as India's main financial and port center, inherited from its colonial position as capital of the Bombay Presidency, is also why so much of its urban growth has concentrated along a narrow coastal strip rather than a spread-out metro region.
cryptic_clue: Named for a local goddess, this city began as seven separate islands, reclaimed and stitched into one. It's now home to a film industry whose nickname rhymes with Hollywood's.
image_caption: Wide skyline view of South Mumbai, India

name: Dubai
peak_smog_season: Summer Arabian desert dust storms & vehicle exhaust

analogue_current.note: Hyper-arid Persian Gulf coastal desert.

analogue_2050.note: Extreme summer heat surpassing 48°C wet-bulb limits.

urban_fact: A fast-growing desert metropolis stretches along the Gulf coast and major highway corridors.
educational_debrief: Dubai grew from a small pearling and fishing settlement on a tidal creek into a major regional trade and finance hub over just a few decades, a transformation driven initially by port and free-trade policies rather than the oil wealth more associated with neighboring emirates. Because it sits in a hot desert climate with almost no reliable freshwater source, the city depends on energy-intensive seawater desalination for most of its drinking water, leaving it acutely exposed to any future stress on that supply chain. Its urban form — a long ribbon of development stretched along the coast and major highways rather than a compact core — reflects how quickly the city expanded outward once large-scale land reclamation and highway building began in earnest.
cryptic_clue: The world's tallest building anchors a desert skyline that also hosts an indoor ski slope and a palm-shaped island reclaimed from the open sea.
image_caption: Downtown Dubai skyline with the Burj Khalifa, seen from a helicopter

name: Cairo
peak_smog_season: Autumn "Black Cloud" agricultural burning & desert dust

analogue_current.note: Nile Valley subtropical hyper-arid.

analogue_2050.note: Hot desert with severe summer temperatures >43°C.

urban_fact: The urban region is concentrated along the Nile and delta edge, sharply bordered by desert.
educational_debrief: Cairo's entire urban footprint is possible only because of the Nile: the city and its farmland give way abruptly to open desert just beyond the river's floodplain and irrigation reach, producing one of the sharpest urban–desert boundaries of any major city on Earth. Egypt draws the overwhelming majority of its fresh water from the Nile, and with population growth, a hot desert climate, and competing demands upstream all bearing on that single source, Cairo is considered one of the more water-stressed major cities anywhere. The city's core still reflects more than a thousand years of continuous settlement as an Islamic capital, layered beneath a 20th-century wave of rapid, often informal expansion that made greater Cairo one of the most densely populated urban regions in the world.
cryptic_clue: On its outskirts stand the last of antiquity's seven wonders still mostly intact. Their afternoon shadows fall toward a capital whose name means 'the victorious.'
image_caption: Skyline of Cairo, Egypt, viewed from Cairo Tower

name: Cape Town
peak_smog_season: Winter valley inversions & summer veld fires

analogue_current.note: Atlantic Mediterranean cool-summer marine.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter Mediterranean summers with reduced winter rain.

urban_fact: Table Mountain, the Atlantic coast, and False Bay divide the city into distinct urban corridors.
educational_debrief: Cape Town was founded in 1652 as a supply station for Dutch East India Company ships rounding the Cape on the route to Asia, making it one of the oldest colonial port settlements in southern Africa and the origin point of the city's historic core beneath Table Mountain. Apartheid-era planning laws forcibly separated communities by race and relocated many non-white residents to new townships on the flat, sandy Cape Flats well outside the city center, a spatial pattern that still shapes commuting patterns and inequality across the metro today. In 2018, Cape Town came close to becoming the first major city to run out of municipal water entirely, a crisis known as 'Day Zero' that was narrowly averted through severe rationing — a stark preview of the water stress its dry-summer Mediterranean climate keeps putting on the city.
cryptic_clue: A flat-topped mountain looks down on a bay where a small offshore island once held the twentieth century's most famous political prisoner for eighteen of his twenty-seven years behind bars.
image_caption: Cape Town skyline with Table Mountain, South Africa

name: Nairobi
peak_smog_season: Dry season unpaved road dust & traffic congestion

analogue_current.note: East African equatorial highland plateau.

analogue_2050.note: Mild highland climate with increased rainfall intensity.

urban_fact: A high-elevation inland city has expanded outward from a rail-era centre beside a national park.
educational_debrief: Nairobi began in 1899 as a supply depot and railhead on the line then being built between Mombasa and Kampala, sited on the plateau roughly halfway along the route for its cool climate and reliable water rather than around any existing settlement. That founding logic still shows: sitting well over 1,600 meters above sea level keeps the city mild and spring-like year-round despite lying almost exactly on the equator, nothing like the tropical heat its latitude alone would suggest. Nairobi also hosts the headquarters of two United Nations agencies, UNEP and UN-Habitat, making it one of the relatively few UN headquarters cities located outside Europe or North America.
cryptic_clue: Its name comes from a Maasai phrase for 'cool water.' It's the only capital on the planet with a national park — lions included — inside the city limits.
image_caption: Nairobi skyline from Uhuru Park, with the KICC building and Times Tower, Kenya

name: Lagos
peak_smog_season: Winter dry Harmattan dust haze & generator fumes

analogue_current.note: Gulf of Guinea wet tropical coastal lagoon.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified tropical coastal humidity and precipitation.

urban_fact: A low-lying lagoon metropolis spans islands, wetlands, bridges, and a rapidly expanding mainland.
educational_debrief: Lagos was Nigeria's capital until the government relocated to the purpose-built city of Abuja near the end of the 20th century, a move partly intended to ease pressure on a city that, even then, was already outgrowing its lagoon-and-island geography. Much of the metropolis sits barely above sea level around Lagos Lagoon, with newer growth pushing onto reclaimed land and low-lying wetlands that leave the city highly exposed to flooding from both storm surge and heavy rain. As West Africa's largest commercial and port city, Lagos has kept drawing migrants from across the region even after losing its status as the seat of government, making it one of the fastest-growing large cities in the world.
cryptic_clue: Portuguese sailors named it for its lagoons. Now the continent's most populous city sprawls across islands stitched together by bridges — and isn't even its own country's capital anymore.
image_caption: Skyline of Lagos, Nigeria

name: Johannesburg
peak_smog_season: Winter highveld thermal inversion & mine dump dust

analogue_current.note: Highveld plateau subtropical highland.

analogue_2050.note: Shifts toward warmer subtropical climate.

urban_fact: A high-altitude, inland urban region grew from a mining belt into a dispersed polycentric metropolis.
educational_debrief: Johannesburg is often cited as the largest city in the world not built beside a river, lake, or coastline — it sits on a watershed divide on the high veld, which is why its water has always had to be piped in from elsewhere, today largely via the Vaal River system and the Lesotho Highlands Water Project rather than any local source. The 1886 discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand reef drew prospectors so fast that a mining camp grew into a city almost before it had a plan, and the mine dumps and tailings left behind by more than a century of gold mining still ring parts of the metro and add to its wintertime dust. Economic activity has since dispersed away from that original mining-era core into newer nodes such as Sandton, leaving greater Johannesburg with a decentralized, multi-centered form rather than one dominant downtown.
cryptic_clue: A gold reef discovered in 1886 conjured this city out of the high veld almost overnight. Locals still call it the City of Gold, though no navigable river runs through it.
image_caption: Johannesburg city skyline at night, South Africa

name: Alexandria
peak_smog_season: Winter industrial emissions & spring Khamasin dust

analogue_current.note: Mediterranean coastal desert margin.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer coastal desert with reduced winter storms.

urban_fact: A long, narrow city follows the Mediterranean shoreline between the sea and inland lakes.
educational_debrief: Alexandria was founded in 331 BCE by Alexander the Great on the narrow strip of land between the Mediterranean and Lake Mariout, and under the Ptolemaic dynasty that followed him it grew into one of the ancient world's great centers of learning, home to the Library of Alexandria and the research institute, the Musaeum, built around it. That same low, narrow coastal position — barely above sea level today — leaves the modern city acutely exposed to Mediterranean storm surge and long-term sea-level rise, and Egyptian authorities have already reinforced long stretches of its shoreline with concrete breakwaters to slow erosion. The city's Corniche waterfront and its dense, elongated footprint both still trace the same narrow coastal strip that shaped Alexandria's layout in antiquity.
cryptic_clue: A conqueror founded this Mediterranean port and stamped it with his own name. Its ancient lighthouse, once one of antiquity's great wonders, is gone; divers now explore what's left of it offshore.
image_caption: The Corniche of Alexandria along the Mediterranean Sea, Egypt

name: New York City
peak_smog_season: Summer high heat & ozone non-attainment days

analogue_current.note: Mid-Atlantic coastal humid subtropical.

analogue_2050.note: Southern humid subtropical conditions with higher humidity.

urban_fact: A harbour metropolis spans islands and peninsulas, linked by an extensive rail and bridge network.
educational_debrief: New York City's five boroughs were once separate municipalities — including the City of Brooklyn, then one of the largest cities in the US in its own right — before they consolidated into a single city at the very end of the 19th century. Much of Manhattan's regular street grid dates to an 1811 plan that imposed a uniform grid over the island's hills and streams well ahead of the development that would eventually fill it. Built across islands, peninsulas, and reclaimed shoreline at the mouth of the Hudson, the city sits low against the harbor, and Hurricane Sandy in 2012 demonstrated just how exposed its subway tunnels and coastal neighborhoods are to storm surge.
cryptic_clue: A copper-green matron has greeted harbour-bound ships for over a century; the boroughs at her back still carry a duke's borrowed name.
image_caption: Midtown Manhattan Commissioners' grid in New York City, USA

name: Los Angeles
peak_smog_season: Late summer/autumn wildfire smoke & photochemical basin smog

analogue_current.note: Southern California Mediterranean coastal.

analogue_2050.note: Arid shift with hotter inland valley extremes.

urban_fact: A broad polycentric basin is bounded by mountains and the Pacific, with development following freeways.
educational_debrief: Los Angeles grew first along an extensive early-20th-century streetcar network — the Pacific Electric 'Red Car' system, once one of the largest interurban rail systems in the world — before that network was dismantled and the region rebuilt itself around the freeway and the private automobile, producing the sprawling, polycentric urban form the city is known for today. Because the local basin receives relatively little natural rainfall for a metropolis its size, Los Angeles has depended since the early 1900s on water imported from hundreds of kilometers away, most famously the Los Angeles Aqueduct that diverted water from the Owens Valley — a project so contentious it triggered decades of legal and physical conflict over water rights. That reliance on imported water, combined with a Mediterranean climate of dry summers, is central to why the city faces some of the most acute long-term water-stress projections of any major US metro.
cryptic_clue: Spanish founders named it for the angels. Today the hills above spell out a global entertainment industry’s name in giant white letters, while Ice Age fossils still bubble out of tar pits in a park downtown.
image_caption: Skyline of Downtown Los Angeles, California, USA

name: Chicago
peak_smog_season: Summer lake-breeze trapped ozone & winter fine particulates

analogue_current.note: Great Lakes humid continental regime.

analogue_2050.note: Midwest humid subtropical shift with hotter summers.

urban_fact: A strong orthogonal grid meets Lake Michigan, with radial rail lines converging on the central business district.
educational_debrief: Chicago is often credited as the birthplace of the modern skyscraper: after the Great Fire of 1871 leveled much of the city, architects rebuilding it pioneered steel-frame construction techniques — beginning with buildings like the Home Insurance Building in the 1880s — that let structures rise far higher than traditional load-bearing walls allowed. The 1909 Plan of Chicago, one of the first comprehensive city plans in the United States, deliberately reserved the entire lakefront for public parks rather than private development, which is why the city's Lake Michigan shoreline remains largely open green space instead of the private waterfronts common in many other lakeside or coastal cities. That combination of a rigid inland street grid and a preserved public lakefront still defines Chicago's layout, with rail lines converging radially on the downtown Loop, which took its name from the elevated tracks encircling it.
cryptic_clue: Its name comes from a Native word for wild onion, once abundant along its river. A lakefront blaze levelled it in 1871, and it rose again home to some of the world’s first skyscrapers.
image_caption: Chicago skyline from North Avenue Beach Pier on Lake Michigan, USA

name: Toronto
peak_smog_season: Summer high-humidity ozone & transboundary wildfire haze

analogue_current.note: Eastern Canadian Great Lakes continental.

analogue_2050.note: Significantly warmer winters and hot continental summers.

urban_fact: A lakefront core anchors a larger polycentric region structured by ravines, railways, and highways.
educational_debrief: Toronto's spread-out grid is really a patchwork of neighbourhoods stitched together across dozens of wooded ravines, carved by post-glacial meltwater rivers that still thread through the city today. Waves of immigration have made roughly half its residents foreign-born, a pattern visible in the ethnic commercial strips lining its arterial roads outside the lakefront core. Lake Ontario currently moderates its humid continental climate, but that climate is projected to shift toward the hot-summer subtype more typical of cities further south by 2050.
cryptic_clue: A slender concrete needle just over 500 metres tall stood as the world’s tallest freestanding structure for more than three decades. Roughly half the people living beneath it today were born somewhere else entirely.
image_caption: Toronto skyline looking west at dawn, with the CN Tower, Canada

name: Mexico City
peak_smog_season: Spring dry season thermal inversions & valley trapped ozone

analogue_current.note: Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt high-altitude valley.

analogue_2050.note: Warm subtropical highland with intensified water scarcity.

urban_fact: One of the world’s largest high-altitude urban regions occupies a mountain-ringed former lake basin.
educational_debrief: Mexico City rises on the drained bed of Lake Texcoco, the shallow basin the Aztecs turned into the island capital Tenochtitlan using causeways and chinampas before Spanish colonizers drained the lake outright to control flooding. Because much of the city still sits on that former lakebed, groundwater pumping from the aquifer beneath it causes ongoing subsidence, visible in tilted buildings across the historic center. Its high-altitude basin, ringed by volcanoes, already traps pollution, and by 2050 the same closed geography is projected to concentrate severe water stress as demand keeps outpacing a shrinking aquifer.
cryptic_clue: Legend says an eagle perched on a cactus, devouring a serpent, told wandering Aztec settlers where to build their island capital. Centuries later, a colonial cathedral rose from the stones of the great pyramid it replaced.
image_caption: Paseo de la Reforma skyline and Chapultepec Park, Mexico City

name: Vancouver
peak_smog_season: Late summer Pacific Northwest wildfire smoke events

analogue_current.note: Pacific Northwest marine rainforest.

analogue_2050.note: Drier, sunnier Mediterranean-trending summers.

urban_fact: Dense centres and suburbs fit between the Pacific, the Fraser River, and steep coastal mountains.
educational_debrief: Vancouver is boxed into a narrow strip of buildable land between the Pacific, the Fraser River delta, and the steep Coast Mountains, which is part of why its downtown grew densely vertical instead of sprawling outward like most North American cities. That mild, wet setting has also made it one of North America's busiest film and television production hubs, standing in on-screen for dozens of other cities. Climate models project its summers drying and warming toward a Mediterranean-type climate by mid-century, an unusual shift for a city this far north.
cryptic_clue: Named for the British captain who charted its coast, this Pacific film hub doubles for a hundred other cities on screen and once hosted the world under five interlocked rings in the snow.
image_caption: Aerial view of downtown Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada

name: Buenos Aires
peak_smog_season: Winter calm wind conditions & Paraná delta burning

analogue_current.note: Río de la Plata estuary humid subtropical.

analogue_2050.note: Subtropical marine climate with hotter summer peaks.

urban_fact: A vast regular grid spreads from the Río de la Plata, interrupted by rail corridors and suburban centres.
educational_debrief: Buenos Aires spreads from the Río de la Plata as a strict, regular grid, a Spanish colonial planning pattern later broken up by rail lines and satellite town centers as the city grew outward. Its estuary setting exposes it to the sudestada, a southeasterly storm that pushes river water back into low-lying coastal barrios, a flood risk distinct from ordinary rainfall. The city's dense Italian and Spanish immigrant heritage also shaped its most famous cultural export, tango, which developed in its working-class port neighborhoods in the late 19th century.
cryptic_clue: Its own name translates to ‘fair winds.’ A pink presidential palace faces an avenue often called the widest in the world, in the city where tango was born.
image_caption: Panorama of Puerto Madero, Buenos Aires, Argentina, in the morning

name: São Paulo
peak_smog_season: Winter dry season vehicle thermal inversion

analogue_current.note: Southern Brazilian highland subtropical.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer tropical highland with intense summer convection.

urban_fact: A huge inland metropolis covers a hilly plateau, with dense corridors following rivers and transport infrastructure.
educational_debrief: São Paulo grew on an inland plateau far from any coast, so unlike Brazil's beach-facing cities its urban form follows rivers, rail lines, and highway corridors rather than a shoreline. Chronic gridlock across a metropolis of more than twenty million has pushed the wealthy toward helicopters for short hops between office towers, giving the city one of the largest private helicopter fleets in the world. It was founded by Jesuit missionaries in 1554 on the feast day marking the apostle Paul's conversion, a name that long outlasted its modest origins as a hilltop mission post.
cryptic_clue: Named for the apostle converted on the road to Damascus, this inland metropolis reportedly has more helicopters landing on its rooftops than almost anywhere else on Earth.
image_caption: Aerial drone view of the São Paulo skyline above Parque da Aclimação, Brazil

name: Rio de Janeiro
peak_smog_season: Summer high heat and humidity ozone buildup

analogue_current.note: Atlantic tropical coastal bay.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter tropical conditions with sustained humidity.

urban_fact: Mountains, bays, beaches, and lagoons divide the city into dramatic, discontinuous urban districts.
educational_debrief: Rio de Janeiro's granite peaks, bays, and coastal lagoons carve the city into separated pockets of development rather than one continuous built-up area, a morphology dictated almost entirely by its geology. Portuguese explorers mistook the entrance to Guanabara Bay for a river mouth and named the settlement for the month they arrived, January — a naming error that stuck permanently. The Christ the Redeemer statue atop Corcovado mountain, completed in 1931, has become a defining symbol of a city where informal hillside favela settlements and formal beachfront neighborhoods sit within sight of each other yet remain sharply divided by elevation and access.
cryptic_clue: Sailors mistook a bay for a river’s mouth and named the place for the month they arrived. A stone giant with outstretched arms now watches its beaches from a mountain whose name means ‘hunchback.’
image_caption: Panoramic view of Rio de Janeiro captured from the top of Sugarloaf Mountain, Brazil

name: Lima
peak_smog_season: Winter garúa fog trapping vehicle exhaust under marine inversion

analogue_current.note: Peruvian coastal desert under cold Humboldt Current.

analogue_2050.note: Warming coastal desert with persistent marine cloud.

urban_fact: A desert coastal metropolis expands across river valleys beneath persistent Pacific marine cloud.
educational_debrief: Lima is a true desert capital: despite sitting almost on the Pacific and holding more than eleven million people, it receives so little rain that the city depends on rivers descending from the Andes and a near-permanent low cloud deck, the garúa, for what little moisture reaches it. The Spanish founded it as the 'City of Kings' in 1535, and the name Lima gradually wore down from Rímac, the indigenous name of the river cutting through the city. That colonial-era prominence also gave Lima the National University of San Marcos, founded in 1551 and among the oldest universities in the Americas.
cryptic_clue: Conquistadors called it the City of Kings, though everyday use wore that down into a mangled version of the river running through it. One of the oldest universities in the Americas has operated here since the 1550s.
image_caption: Costa Verde coastline and skyline of the Miraflores district, Lima, Peru

name: Bogotá
peak_smog_season: Early dry season thermal inversions in the high Andean basin

analogue_current.note: High-altitude equatorial Andean plateau.

analogue_2050.note: Isothermal mountain climate with higher mean temperatures.

urban_fact: A dense high-altitude city stretches north–south along a plateau against the eastern Andes.
educational_debrief: Bogotá sits on a high Andean plateau above 2,500 meters, cool enough year-round that its climate reads as oceanic despite lying almost on the equator — altitude, not latitude, sets its temperature here. The city's name descends from Bacatá, a Muisca chiefdom that ruled the plateau before Spanish conquest. Nearby Lake Guatavita, where Muisca leaders once ritually covered themselves in gold dust before bathing, gave rise to the El Dorado legend that drew European explorers across South America for generations.
cryptic_clue: A Muisca chiefdom’s name, worn down by Spanish tongues, became this plateau capital’s own. Nearby, a golden king once bathed in a mountain lake, seeding the legend of a lost city of gold.
image_caption: Downtown Bogotá skyline at dusk, Colombia

name: Sydney
peak_smog_season: Summer bushfire smoke events & basin ozone accumulation

analogue_current.note: East coast Australian humid subtropical.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer subtropical summers with increased extreme heat days.

urban_fact: A branching drowned-river harbour, coastal bays, and sandstone terrain fragment the urban footprint.
educational_debrief: Sydney's suburbs are broken into an unusually fragmented patchwork by the deeply indented, drowned river valley of its harbour and the sandstone ridges and gullies of the surrounding basin, forcing roads and rail lines to bend around bays and headlands rather than run in straight lines. The city began as a British penal colony at the harbour's edge in the late 18th century, and that original settlement site — chosen for its deep, sheltered anchorage — remains the dense heart of the modern metropolis. Because harbour and coastline border so much of the urban area, Sydney's bushfire-prone hinterland and beach-lined shore give it both scenic value and recurring exposure to fire and coastal weather extremes.
cryptic_clue: Named for a British home secretary, this harbour city’s coat-hanger-shaped bridge and a cluster of white sails on the water’s edge are recognised on sight almost anywhere.
image_caption: Sydney Opera House and Harbour Bridge at dusk, Australia
image_author: Benh LIEU SONG via Wikimedia Commons

name: Melbourne
peak_smog_season: Summer northerly desert winds & winter wood smoke

analogue_current.note: Port Phillip temperate maritime.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, drier conditions with sharp hot spikes.

urban_fact: A broad, relatively flat metropolis uses a strong central grid and radial rail corridors around Port Phillip.
educational_debrief: Melbourne's central grid, laid out in the 1830s, expanded outward along radial rail and tram lines rather than a single dominant highway corridor, leaving it with one of the largest urban tram networks in the world. Named for a 19th-century British prime minister, the city grew rapidly during Victoria's gold rush and has since repeatedly topped global liveability rankings, a reputation often credited to that dense transit and green-space legacy around Port Phillip Bay. Its climate is projected to shift from oceanic toward humid subtropical by mid-century as its temperate summers warm.
cryptic_clue: Named for a British prime minister, this city runs one of the world’s largest urban tram networks and topped global liveability rankings for seven years running.
image_caption: Melbourne CBD skyline and the Yarra River as seen from Southbank, Australia

name: Auckland
peak_smog_season: Winter calm mornings with localized domestic wood smoke

analogue_current.note: New Zealand North Island maritime temperate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer subtropical marine conditions.

urban_fact: A narrow volcanic isthmus between two harbours produces a linear, water-defined urban region.
educational_debrief: Auckland occupies a narrow volcanic isthmus only a few kilometers wide at its narrowest point, squeezed between two harbours, which forces its urban area into a long, water-constrained shape rather than spreading freely in every direction. That isthmus is dotted with dozens of dormant volcanic cones, remnants of the same eruptions that built the land the city stands on. Auckland also holds the largest Polynesian population of any city on Earth, reflecting deep and ongoing ties across the Pacific alongside its more recent identity as the 'City of Sails.'
cryptic_clue: Nicknamed for its sails, this harbour city claims more boats per person than almost anywhere else, and its population makes it the largest Polynesian city on Earth.
image_caption: Skyline of Auckland City with Mt. Eden in the foreground and the Harbour Bridge in the background, New Zealand
image_author: Christian Mehlführer, reworked by Ralf Roletschek, via Wikimedia Commons

name: Perth
peak_smog_season: Summer easterly winds with hot desert dust & prescribed burns

analogue_current.note: Southern hemisphere Mediterranean west coast.

analogue_2050.note: Hot, dry Mediterranean regime with intensified summer drought.

urban_fact: A low-density coastal metropolis extends along the Indian Ocean between the Swan River and inland escarpment.
educational_debrief: Perth is routinely cited as one of the most isolated major cities on Earth, with its nearest big-city neighbor lying more than two thousand kilometers away across largely empty desert. That isolation historically pushed the city toward low-density, car-oriented growth along the Swan River and Indian Ocean coast rather than a denser form. Its Mediterranean-type climate, with dry summers, already strains water supply, and the city responded by opening one of Australia's earliest large-scale seawater desalination plants to reduce reliance on a shrinking aquifer.
cryptic_clue: Named for a Scottish city on another continent, this is often called the most isolated major city on Earth — its nearest big-city neighbour lies over two thousand kilometres away.
image_caption: Perth CBD skyline viewed from Kings Park, Western Australia

name: Adelaide
peak_smog_season: Summer northerly desert heatwaves & winter woodsmoke

analogue_current.note: Mediterranean dry summer climate.

analogue_2050.note: Semi-arid transition with severe summer heatwaves.

urban_fact: A planned central grid is enclosed by a continuous park belt, with suburbs between the coast and Mount Lofty Ranges.
educational_debrief: Adelaide was laid out in 1837 to a single deliberate plan by colonial surveyor William Light: a strict central grid completely encircled by a ring of parkland that remains intact today, one of the most intentional pieces of city planning from that era. Nicknamed the City of Churches for the density of 19th-century congregations it once supported, it now also hosts the Adelaide Fringe, the second-largest arts festival of its kind in the world after Edinburgh's. Its Mediterranean-type climate is projected to dry further into a semi-arid regime by 2050, consistent with the water stress already building across South Australia.
cryptic_clue: Named for a queen consort, this planned coastal capital is nicknamed the City of Churches and stages the second-largest fringe arts festival in the world every year.
image_caption: Aerial view of the Adelaide skyline and the River Torrens, South Australia

name: Stockholm
peak_smog_season: Spring studded-tyre road dust & winter wood-smoke inversions

analogue_current.note: Baltic hemiboreal climate with cold winters and mild, humid summers.

analogue_2050.note: Milder oceanic winters as continental cold retreats.

urban_fact: Stockholm spans fourteen islands linked by more than fifty bridges where Lake Mälaren meets the Baltic archipelago.
educational_debrief: Stockholm is built across fourteen islands where Lake Mälaren drains into the Baltic archipelago, a fragmented geography stitched together by more than fifty bridges. Its old town, Gamla Stan, still follows medieval street patterns dating to the city's founding as a fortified trading post in the 13th century. Each December the city hosts the Nobel Prize ceremonies, honoring laureates in science, literature, and peace under the terms of Swedish industrialist Alfred Nobel's will.
cryptic_clue: Its name is said to mean simply ‘log islet.’ Every December, this archipelago capital hosts the world’s most famous prize ceremony, honouring laureates in science, literature, and peace.
image_caption: Skeppsbrokajen waterfront in Stockholm, seen from Skeppsholmen with Gamla Stan (Old Town) behind it, Sweden

name: Moscow
peak_smog_season: Summer wildfire smoke haze & winter temperature-inversion smog

analogue_current.note: East European continental climate with a similar cold-winter, warm-summer cycle.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter continental summers under a shorter, milder winter regime.

urban_fact: Concentric ring roads — the Boulevard Ring, Garden Ring, and outer MKAD — trace Moscow’s growth outward from the Kremlin along the Moskva River.
educational_debrief: Moscow's ring-upon-ring street pattern — the Boulevard Ring, the Garden Ring, and the outer MKAD motorway — traces nearly nine centuries of growth outward from the Kremlin, interrupted by a roughly two-century stretch when Russia's capital moved to St. Petersburg and Moscow's growth slowed. The city's continental climate brings a wide swing between cold winters and warm summers, a seasonal extremity typical of interior cities far from any moderating coastline. Much of Moscow's Soviet-era growth beyond the historic ring roads took the form of large standardized housing districts, or microrayons, built rapidly to house a fast-expanding industrial workforce — a pattern that still shapes the outer city today.
cryptic_clue: Named for the river it sits beside, its central square is watched over by a candy-striped cathedral of onion domes, and its subway stations are ornate enough to double as museums.
image_caption: View of the Moscow Kremlin from the river near Bolshoy Kamenny Bridge, Russia

name: Bucharest
peak_smog_season: Winter residential-heating inversion & summer traffic ozone

analogue_current.note: Balkan continental climate with hot, humid summers and cold winters.

analogue_2050.note: Po Valley humid subtropical regime with hot, muggy summers.

urban_fact: Broad boulevards radiate from a Belle Époque core once nicknamed “Little Paris,” later reshaped by Ceaușescu-era socialist redevelopment.
educational_debrief: Bucharest's boulevards radiate outward from a core so lavishly rebuilt in the Belle Époque style that the city earned the nickname 'Little Paris' in the early 20th century. That fabric was cut through in the 1980s when Nicolae Ceaușescu demolished large parts of the historic center to build the monumental Palace of the Parliament, widely cited as the heaviest administrative building in the world, along with the wide socialist-era boulevards surrounding it. The city's own name is traditionally traced to Bucur, a legendary shepherd said to have founded a settlement on the site long before its first recorded mention.
cryptic_clue: Legend credits a shepherd named Bucur as its founder, and the city may still carry his name. A paranoid dictator later built what’s recognised as the heaviest building on Earth as his own palace.
image_caption: Bucharest skyline from the Intercontinental Hotel, showing University Square and the Palace of the Parliament, Romania

name: Istanbul
peak_smog_season: Winter coal and wood heating inversion across the Bosphorus valley

analogue_current.note: Northern Aegean hot-summer Mediterranean climate.

analogue_2050.note: Anatolian semi-arid conditions with drier, hotter summers.

urban_fact: The Bosphorus strait splits the city between Europe and Asia, with the Golden Horn carving a historic harbour into the European side.
educational_debrief: Istanbul is the only major city built across two continents, split by the Bosphorus strait connecting the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara, with the Golden Horn inlet carving a natural harbor into its European side. Founded as Byzantium and later renamed Constantinople after the Roman emperor who made it his capital, the city's Hagia Sophia has served in turn as a cathedral, a mosque, a museum, and a mosque again since its completion in the 6th century. Its Mediterranean-type climate is projected to shift toward semi-arid conditions by 2050, adding pressure to a water system already straining to serve a metropolis of nearly sixteen million.
cryptic_clue: Once Byzantium, then a Roman emperor’s namesake, this is the only major city straddling two continents. A sixth-century domed cathedral-turned-mosque still dominates its skyline.
image_caption: Aerial view of the historical peninsula and modern skyline of Istanbul, Turkey

name: Lisbon
peak_smog_season: Summer Saharan heat plumes & wildfire smoke episodes

analogue_current.note: Atlantic-moderated Mediterranean climate on the strait.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, drier semi-arid regime with intensified summer heat.

urban_fact: Seven hills frame Lisbon’s amphitheatre-like waterfront where the wide Tagus estuary opens into the Atlantic.
educational_debrief: Lisbon's seven hills frame an amphitheater-like waterfront where the wide Tagus estuary meets the Atlantic, a setting that once made the city a natural launch point for Portuguese Age of Discovery voyages. A massive earthquake and tsunami devastated Lisbon on All Saints' Day in 1755, and the chief minister who rebuilt it, the Marquês de Pombal, pioneered a timber-braced construction technique designed to flex rather than collapse in future tremors — among the earliest examples of engineered earthquake-resistant urban planning anywhere. Its Mediterranean climate is projected to shift toward semi-arid by 2050, part of a broader drying trend across the Iberian Peninsula.
cryptic_clue: A limestone tower once watched caravels sail west for coasts no European chart yet showed. When a Sunday earthquake and tsunami flattened the city in 1755, its chief minister rebuilt the center on a timber-braced grid engineered to sway, not shatter — one of the world's first quake-resistant downtowns.
image_caption: Panoramic view of Lisbon and the Ponte 25 de Abril over the Tagus River, seen from Cristo Rei, Portugal

name: Vienna
peak_smog_season: Winter Danube valley temperature inversion

analogue_current.note: Danube-basin temperate climate just downstream.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, more humid subtropical-leaning summers.

urban_fact: The Ringstrasse boulevard traces the line of Vienna’s medieval walls, encircling the historic core beside the Danube.
educational_debrief: Vienna's Ringstrasse boulevard traces the exact footprint of the medieval fortifications that once encircled the city, demolished in the 1850s and replaced with grand public buildings and parks in a single coordinated redevelopment. Legend credits the retreating Ottoman army from the 1683 siege of Vienna with leaving behind sacks of coffee beans, seeding a coffeehouse culture the city still treats as a defining institution. That same dense, walkable core produced an outsized share of the Western classical music canon, from Mozart and Beethoven to the Strauss family waltzes.
cryptic_clue: Legend holds that when a besieging army fled in 1683, it left behind sacks of a strange bean — and the coffeehouse culture born from it is now protected as UNESCO intangible heritage. The same streets produced more waltzes, string quartets, and psychoanalysts per capita than seems reasonable for the size of the place.
image_caption: The Vienna skyline as seen from the Alte Donau in Donaustadt, Austria

name: Tehran
peak_smog_season: Winter temperature-inversion smog trapped by the Alborz foothills

analogue_current.note: Semi-arid highland capital with cold winters and hot, dry summers.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter, drier semi-arid conditions with intensified summer heat.

urban_fact: Tehran climbs the southern slopes of the Alborz range, its historic qanat channels once carrying mountain meltwater into a dry basin city.
educational_debrief: Tehran climbs the southern slopes of the Alborz mountains, and that elevation gradient sorts the city both socially and thermally: wealthier neighborhoods sit higher on the cooler northern slopes, while poorer districts spread across the hotter, smog-trapped basin to the south. The city's historic qanats — gently sloping underground channels that carried mountain meltwater into the dry basin by gravity alone — once supplied much of its water before modern pumping took over. Its steppe climate is projected to shift from cold to hot semi-arid by 2050, compounding water stress in a city already relying on a shrinking supply.
cryptic_clue: A white marble arch, built to mark an empire's twenty-five-hundredth anniversary, guards the western approach to a capital pressed against a jagged mountain wall. Its wealthier quarters climb the cool northern slopes; the older, poorer half spreads south into the smog.
image_caption: Tehran skyline viewed from Milad Tower, Iran

name: Almaty
peak_smog_season: Winter temperature-inversion smog trapped against the Tian Shan foothills

analogue_current.note: Tian Shan foothill continental climate just across the range.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer Central Asian continental climate with hotter summers.

urban_fact: A strict grid of tree-lined avenues climbs the alluvial slopes below the Tian Shan foothills, with mountain streams channelled along many streets.
educational_debrief: Almaty's name translates roughly to 'father of apples,' and the wild apple forests in the Tian Shan foothills above the city are recognized by botanists as a likely ancestral source of the domesticated apples eaten worldwide today. The city's strict grid of tree-lined avenues climbs the alluvial slopes below those mountains, with meltwater streams historically channeled along many streets for irrigation and cooling. Almaty served as Kazakhstan's capital until 1997, when the government relocated to a purpose-built city, now Astana, further north on the steppe.
cryptic_clue: Its name translates roughly to 'father of apples,' and the wild orchards in the foothills above it are now recognized as the ancestral source of nearly every apple eaten on the planet. It was once its country's capital, before government moved to a newly built city out on the northern steppe.
image_caption: City skyline of Almaty viewed from the Kök Töbe hilltop, Kazakhstan

name: Baku
peak_smog_season: Summer stagnant-air industrial haze from Absheron refineries

analogue_current.note: Caspian-basin semi-arid climate with mild winters and hot summers.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter semi-arid conditions with intensified summer heat.

urban_fact: A crescent-shaped natural harbour on the Caspian Sea shelters Baku’s walled Old City beside oil-boom-era boulevards.
educational_debrief: Baku sits on a crescent-shaped natural harbor on the Caspian Sea and is widely cited as the only national capital in the world that lies below sea level. Naturally seeping underground gas has burned in spots around the region for centuries, giving rise to the old name 'land of fire' long before the city's 19th- and early 20th-century oil boom financed the grand boulevards that still ring its walled Old City. That oil wealth also underwrote the more recent Flame Towers skyline, a modern echo of the same fire imagery.
cryptic_clue: Long before its skyline sprouted three glass towers shaped like flames, natural gas seeping from the ground nearby burned steadily enough that early travelers called this the land of fire. It's also widely cited as the only national capital that sits below sea level.
image_caption: Panoramic view of Baku, showing the Flame Towers and the Caspian Sea coastline, Azerbaijan

name: Ulaanbaatar
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-stove ger-district smog trapped by valley temperature inversions

analogue_current.note: Inner Mongolian steppe continental climate with a dry, cold winter.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer continental climate as extreme cold retreats.

urban_fact: Ulaanbaatar fills the Tuul River valley between four sacred mountains, its ger districts spreading up the surrounding slopes without formal infrastructure.
educational_debrief: Ulaanbaatar fills the Tuul River valley surrounded by four mountains considered sacred, with informal ger districts — named for the traditional round felt tents many residents still live in — spreading up the surrounding slopes without much formal infrastructure. Before settling permanently on this site, the city began as a mobile Buddhist monastic center that relocated roughly twenty times over more than a century. Its current name, meaning 'Red Hero,' was adopted after the 1920s revolution, and by average annual temperature it remains the coldest national capital on Earth.
cryptic_clue: Its name translates to 'Red Hero,' adopted after a 1920s revolution — though for centuries before that it was a mobile Buddhist monastic center that relocated roughly twenty times before finally settling here for good. By average annual temperature, it's the coldest national capital on Earth.
image_caption: Skyline of Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia

name: Delhi
peak_smog_season: Autumn/winter crop-stubble burning smoke trapped by cold-season thermal inversion

analogue_current.note: Shares the Indo-Gangetic Plain monsoon-influenced subtropical rhythm.

analogue_2050.note: Extreme pre-monsoon heat trending toward semi-arid aridity.

urban_fact: Delhi layers the walled Mughal city of Shahjahanabad, Lutyens's radial New Delhi avenues, and sprawling NCR satellite towns across the Yamuna floodplain.
educational_debrief: Delhi's air quality crisis peaks each autumn when regional crop-residue burning combines with cool, stagnant winter air to trap smoke over the Indo-Gangetic Plain.
cryptic_clue: A wrought-iron pillar has stood in a courtyard here for some 1,600 years without rusting, a metallurgical trick nobody fully explains. The city has also been rebuilt as a dynastic capital so many times that historians count at least seven distinct former cities buried beneath the current one.
image_caption: Old Delhi skyline viewed from Jama Masjid, Delhi, India

name: Dhaka
peak_smog_season: Dry winter (Dec-Feb) brick-kiln emissions trapped under stagnant cool-season air

analogue_current.note: Shares the Bengal delta's wet-dry tropical monsoon rhythm.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified monsoon rainfall and cyclone-linked flooding.

urban_fact: Dhaka grew along the Buriganga River as a Mughal river port and now packs one of the world's highest urban densities into a low-lying Ganges-Brahmaputra delta floodplain.
educational_debrief: Bangladesh's capital sits almost entirely within the world's largest river delta, making land subsidence and monsoon flooding a permanent constraint on how the city can grow.
cryptic_clue: Weavers here once produced cotton so fine an entire garment could be pulled through a finger ring — a craft colonial administrators moved to stamp out because it undercut their own mills back home. These days the same streets are said to carry more human-powered rickshaws than any other city on Earth.
image_caption: Night skyline of Dhaka, Bangladesh, with the Motijheel commercial district
image_author: Md. Ishtiaque Mahmood Rohan via Wikimedia Commons

name: Karachi
peak_smog_season: Winter calm-wind inversions trapping vehicle and industrial smoke along the coast

analogue_current.note: Hot arid Arabian Sea coastal climate with mild maritime moderation.

analogue_2050.note: Extreme combined heat and humidity approaching dangerous wet-bulb levels.

urban_fact: Pakistan's largest city sprawls along a natural harbour on the Arabian Sea, its street grid shaped by British-era cantonments layered over older fishing settlements.
educational_debrief: As Pakistan's main seaport and economic engine, Karachi draws migrants from across the country, producing one of South Asia's most linguistically diverse but infrastructure-strained megacities.
cryptic_clue: This port city briefly served as its young nation's first capital, before the seat of government moved to a purpose-built city further north. Its founder's marble mausoleum — a white parabolic dome, guarded around the clock — anchors a skyline that grew from a small fishing settlement into the country's largest city by far.
image_caption: Clifton skyline in Karachi, Pakistan

name: Kathmandu
peak_smog_season: Dry winter (Dec-Feb) inversion trapping brick-kiln and vehicle smoke inside the valley bowl

analogue_current.note: A mild subtropical highland "City of Eternal Spring" at comparable elevation.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer humid subtropical foothill climate with hotter monsoon summers.

urban_fact: Kathmandu occupies a bowl-shaped Himalayan valley basin, where a dense historic core of Newar courtyards and temples has been engulfed by rapid unplanned sprawl.
educational_debrief: Reconstruction after the 2015 earthquake reshaped parts of the Kathmandu Valley, though many of its historic Newar squares and temple courtyards were painstakingly restored.
cryptic_clue: This city takes its name from a pavilion said to have been built entirely from the timber of a single tree, without a single metal nail. A young girl, chosen through ancient ritual, still lives in a courtyard here, venerated as a living goddess until she reaches puberty.
image_caption: Panoramic view of Kathmandu Valley from Swoyambhu hill, Nepal

name: Bangkok
peak_smog_season: Dry season (Dec-Mar) regional crop burning haze trapped under weak winds

analogue_current.note: Indochina tropical savanna climate with an equally sharp monsoon cycle.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter conditions with a more intense, monsoon-dominated wet season.

urban_fact: Bangkok grew along the meandering Chao Phraya River and a historic network of khlong canals, and keeps subsiding on soft delta clay even as it expands along elevated expressways.
educational_debrief: Bangkok sinks by a few centimetres most years as groundwater is pumped from beneath it, compounding its exposure to Chao Phraya River flooding and a rising Gulf of Thailand.
cryptic_clue: This city's full ceremonial name runs past 160 letters — a Guinness-recognized record for longest place name still in active use — though locals just use a two-syllable nickname instead. A small jade Buddha inside its royal temple complex, and a giant reclining one next door, together draw more visitors than almost any other religious site in the region.
image_caption: Skyline of Bangkok, Thailand, seen from Wat Arun

name: Manila
peak_smog_season: Dry season (Mar-May) vehicle exhaust and construction dust under weak winds

analogue_current.note: Shares the same tropical monsoon rhythm and typhoon exposure.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, more seasonally contrasted monsoon conditions.

urban_fact: Metro Manila wraps Manila Bay and the Pasig River, an amalgam of sixteen cities and municipalities built on reclaimed land and river floodplains prone to subsidence.
educational_debrief: Metro Manila is legally a federation of sixteen cities and one municipality rather than a single administration, complicating coordinated flood control and transit planning.
cryptic_clue: For two and a half centuries, a single annual galleon sailed from this bay to Mexico and back, tying a Pacific colony to the Americas through silver and silk. A quarter here, founded in 1594 to house Chinese merchants, is often called the world's oldest Chinatown.
image_caption: Skyline of Manila along the Pasig River, Philippines

name: Jakarta
peak_smog_season: Dry season (Jun-Sep) traffic emissions and occasional transboundary peatland fire haze

analogue_current.note: Same Java coastal tropical savanna wet-dry cycle.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter, more humid tropical conditions with heavier downpours.

urban_fact: Jakarta spans a low coastal plain crossed by thirteen rivers and canals, and is sinking faster than almost any other major city on Earth from groundwater extraction.
educational_debrief: Jakarta's chronic subsidence and flood risk were central reasons Indonesia began relocating its capital to Nusantara on Borneo, a multi-decade transition still underway.
cryptic_clue: Dutch colonists once ran their entire East Indies trading empire from a port they called Batavia, its canals modeled on Amsterdam's own. Its independence monument today is a marble obelisk crowned with a flame gilded in tens of kilograms of gold, visible for miles across the low delta sprawl around it.
image_caption: Jakarta skyline at golden hour, Indonesia

name: Taipei
peak_smog_season: Winter-spring (Jan-Apr) regional haze and Asian dust under weak monsoon winds

analogue_current.note: Cross-strait humid subtropical climate with a similar typhoon season.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, tropical monsoon-influenced conditions with milder winters.

urban_fact: Taipei fills a mountain-ringed river basin along the Tamsui and Keelung Rivers, its dense low-rise neighbourhoods packed against steep forested slopes at the edges.
educational_debrief: Taipei's basin setting traps summer heat and humidity, but its extensive MRT network and night-market culture make it one of Asia's most walkable capitals — and its winters are warming toward the tropical threshold.
cryptic_clue: A skyscraper here held the world's-tallest title for six years after opening in 2004, and still lets visitors watch its 660-tonne steel pendulum sway inside the building, damping the shock of typhoons and the earthquakes that regularly rattle the mountain-ringed basin beneath it.
image_caption: Night skyline of Taipei, Taiwan, with Taipei 101

name: Honolulu
peak_smog_season: Rare volcanic "vog" haze drifting from Big Island eruptions during trade-wind lulls

analogue_current.note: Trade-wind-moderated tropical coast with a comparably pronounced dry season.

analogue_2050.note: A drier, more pronounced dry-season trade-wind tropical Pacific island climate.

urban_fact: Honolulu occupies a narrow coastal shelf on Oahu between the Koolau Range and the Pacific, its urban core squeezed between Diamond Head, Pearl Harbor, and the sea.
educational_debrief: Honolulu's rainfall varies enormously over short distances, from a few hundred millimetres downtown to several metres a year on the nearby Koolau ridgeline just kilometres away.
cryptic_clue: Its name translates to 'sheltered harbor.' A palace built here for a Pacific kingdom had electric lighting installed before the White House did — a kingdom overthrown a few years later in a coup backed by foreign marines, its grounds now flying a very different flag.
image_caption: Skyline of Honolulu, Hawaii, United States

name: Port Moresby
peak_smog_season: Dry season (Jun-Sep) dust and savanna grass-fire smoke under southeast trade winds

analogue_current.note: A comparably dry tropical savanna climate for its latitude, shaped by rain-shadow effects.

analogue_2050.note: A hotter tropical savanna climate with a far more intense monsoon wet season.

urban_fact: Port Moresby spreads across low hills and bays on the unusually dry, rain-shadowed south coast of Papua New Guinea, its settlements shaped by steep terrain and limited road connections.
educational_debrief: Port Moresby lacks road connections to almost every other town in Papua New Guinea, so most domestic travel and trade still moves by air or coastal shipping.
cryptic_clue: A British naval captain charted this harbour in 1873 and named it after his own father, an admiral who never once set foot here. It anchors a nation that is home to more distinct languages — well over eight hundred — than anywhere else on Earth.
image_caption: Aerial view of Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea

name: Dakar
peak_smog_season: Winter Harmattan dust intrusions blowing off the Sahara (Nov-Mar)

analogue_current.note: Coastal Sahelian hot desert cooled by the same Canary Current upwelling.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified Sahelian heat and a shorter, harder monsoon window.

urban_fact: Dakar occupies the tip of the Cap-Vert peninsula, mainland Africa's westernmost point, its dense colonial-era plateau grid giving way to sprawling suburbs along the narrowing isthmus toward the interior.
educational_debrief: As Senegal's Atlantic gateway, Dakar concentrates the country's port, rail, and air links on a narrow peninsula, so Harmattan dust, sea-level exposure, and rapid in-migration all converge on the same limited land.
cryptic_clue: A short ferry ride offshore sits a small island whose colonial-era holding house and 'Door of No Return' now form one of the most visited memorials to the Atlantic slave trade on the continent. For decades, a grueling off-road motor rally that began each new year in Paris also famously finished on this coastline, lending the race its enduring name.
image_caption: Skyline of Dakar, Senegal, seen from Gorée
image_author: Vincenzo Fotoguru Iaconianni via Wikimedia Commons

name: Accra
peak_smog_season: Winter Harmattan dust haze off the Sahara (Dec-Feb)

analogue_current.note: Same Gulf of Guinea dry corridor with a lighter, more seasonal tropical rainfall regime.

analogue_2050.note: Drier interior savanna conditions with a shortened, more erratic wet season.

urban_fact: Accra grew outward from the historic trading forts of Jamestown and Osu along the Gulf of Guinea, filling in with dense, largely unplanned low-rise neighbourhoods threaded by tro-tro minibus routes.
educational_debrief: Accra sits inside West Africa's Dahomey Gap, a coastal dry corridor that interrupts the humid rainforest belt, giving the city noticeably lighter and more seasonal rainfall than its tropical latitude would suggest.
cryptic_clue: A flag came down and another went up at midnight here in 1957, making this the first sub-Saharan capital to shake off colonial rule — a moment its first president called a turning point for the whole continent. His mausoleum, a black marble monument topped with a star, sits near the parade grounds where that flag changed.
image_caption: Airport City skyline in Accra, Ghana

name: Casablanca
peak_smog_season: Summer Chergui desert winds & winter coastal fog inversion

analogue_current.note: Comparable hot-summer Mediterranean regime moderated by an adjacent coastline.

analogue_2050.note: Semi-arid Mediterranean margin with a much drier, near-desert annual rainfall total.

urban_fact: Casablanca's French-era grid, laid out under architect Henri Prost in the 1910s-20s, radiates from an Art Deco centre toward vast informal peripheries around Africa's busiest Atlantic port.
educational_debrief: Cooled year-round by the Canary Current offshore, Casablanca has notably milder summers than its Saharan-fringe latitude implies, though Morocco's deepening water crisis is now reshaping the wider region's climate risk.
cryptic_clue: A mosque here holds one of the tallest minarets on Earth and juts out over the Atlantic on pillars, its glass floor letting worshippers look down at the waves beneath their feet. A famous 1940s film made this city's name recognizable to millions who've never been anywhere nearby — and who'd be surprised to learn none of it was actually filmed here.
image_caption: Aerial view of Casablanca, Morocco

name: Algiers
peak_smog_season: Summer Saharan Sirocco dust & winter traffic-driven inversion

analogue_current.note: Mediterranean basin twin with a comparable hot, dry-summer seasonal rhythm.

analogue_2050.note: Semi-arid North African coast with sharply reduced winter rainfall.

urban_fact: Algiers rises in a natural amphitheatre around its bay, from the dense whitewashed Casbah at the water's edge to Haussmann-style boulevards terraced up the hillside above.
educational_debrief: Algiers' 'Alger la Blanche' silhouette layers an Ottoman-era citadel, a French colonial extension, and postwar high-rise suburbs onto the steep coastal terrain of the Sahel range overlooking the Mediterranean.
cryptic_clue: For centuries, corsair captains sailed from this harbour to raid Mediterranean shipping and ransom captured sailors, brazen enough that a newly independent United States fought two wars trying to stop it. A future Nobel laureate in literature grew up amid its steep streets and later set his most famous novel along this same coastline.
image_caption: Waterfront view of Algiers, Algeria

name: Luanda
peak_smog_season: Dry cacimbo-season traffic haze & coastal fog inversion (Jun-Sep)

analogue_current.note: A cold-current-cooled coastal desert at a similarly low latitude, mirroring the Benguela effect.

analogue_2050.note: Intensifying coastal aridity as upwelling patterns along the same current shift.

urban_fact: Luanda wraps around a crescent bay sheltered by the narrow Ilha de Luanda sandspit, with the colonial-era baixa giving way to dense hillside musseques built on unplanned land.
educational_debrief: The cold Benguela Current offshore suppresses rainfall and moderates temperatures along the Angolan coast, giving oil-rich Luanda a near-desert climate despite sitting barely nine degrees south of the equator.
cryptic_clue: Founded in 1576, among the oldest European-founded cities in sub-Saharan Africa, oil wealth once made international cost-of-living surveys crown it the priciest city on Earth for expatriates — even as most of the metropolis around it lived nowhere near that kind of money.
image_caption: Fortaleza de São Miguel overlooking the bay at Luanda, Angola

name: Kinshasa
peak_smog_season: Dry-season biomass burning & unpaved-road dust (Jun-Aug)

analogue_current.note: Fellow Congo Basin tropical savanna with the same sharply defined June-August dry season.

analogue_2050.note: Drier interior savanna with a longer dry season and more erratic wet-season onset.

urban_fact: Kinshasa sprawls along the south bank of the wide Pool Malebo on the Congo River, facing Brazzaville directly across the water — the closest pair of national capitals anywhere in the world.
educational_debrief: One of the world's fastest-growing megacities, Kinshasa's population has expanded far faster than its road and housing infrastructure, straining a metropolis originally built for a fraction of its current size.
cryptic_clue: In 1974, a heavyweight title fight nicknamed for its jungle setting was staged here, one of boxing's most iconic fighters reclaiming his crown with a rope-a-dope strategy that's now legend. The city's own name changed a few years earlier, shedding the name of the Belgian king who'd once claimed this entire river basin as his personal property.
image_caption: View over Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo

name: Anchorage
peak_smog_season: Winter temperature inversions trapping vehicle exhaust in ice fog

analogue_current.note: Subarctic continental climate with a comparably short, mild summer.

analogue_2050.note: Milder, wetter maritime-leaning conditions as subarctic winters soften.
