urban_fact: A compact bowl-shaped city fills the coastal plain between Cook Inlet and the Chugach Mountains, built outward from a 1915 Alaska Railroad construction camp and still threaded with moose-inhabited greenbelts.
educational_debrief: Anchorage’s low-density, auto-oriented layout was shaped by railroad platting and postwar military expansion, and it sits on comparatively stable gravel soils that ease foundation work unlike much of permafrost-heavy interior Alaska.
cryptic_clue: In 1964, the second-most powerful earthquake ever recorded leveled parts of this city's downtown — a magnitude at the very edge of what solid ground can survive. It's by far the largest city in its state, yet a much smaller town hundreds of miles away, reachable only by boat or plane, keeps the title of capital.
image_caption: Skyline of downtown Anchorage, Alaska, United States

name: Denver
peak_smog_season: Summer wildfire smoke and Front Range ozone under high pressure

analogue_current.note: High-elevation continental steppe climate with dry, sunny winters.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, drier semi-arid conditions with intensified summer heat.

urban_fact: Downtown’s street grid is rotated roughly 45 degrees to align with the South Platte River and Cherry Creek confluence, meeting the surrounding cardinal-direction suburban grid at a visible seam across the city.
educational_debrief: Founded during the 1858 Pikes Peak Gold Rush at the confluence of the South Platte River and Cherry Creek, Denver later engineered a water supply drawn from distant Rocky Mountain snowpack to sustain growth on the semi-arid high plains.
cryptic_clue: A single step on its state capitol's stairway is engraved to mark the exact point where elevation hits a nice round mile — the nickname stuck. Decades later, its airport was built out on the plains with more land inside its perimeter than the whole of Manhattan.
image_caption: Skyline of Denver, Colorado, United States

name: Miami
peak_smog_season: Summer Saharan dust intrusions and humidity-trapped photochemical haze

analogue_current.note: Caribbean tropical monsoon climate with a similar wet-season rhythm.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter tropical conditions with heavier, more concentrated rainfall.

urban_fact: A narrow, low-lying limestone strip between Biscayne Bay and the Everglades, Miami’s westward growth is legally capped by the Urban Development Boundary, producing a linear north–south metropolis atop a porous, flood-prone aquifer.
educational_debrief: Miami’s permeable limestone bedrock means conventional sea walls cannot fully stop flooding, since rising water can seep upward through the ground itself — a distinctive engineering challenge shaping the city’s adaptation planning.
cryptic_clue: Named for how fast it materialized from swampland once a railroad reached it in 1896, this pastel Art Deco beach strip sits a short flight from Cuba, whose exiles remade its western half into a city within the city, nicknamed for their old capital.
image_caption: Downtown Miami skyline at golden hour, Florida, United States

name: Havana
peak_smog_season: Dry season vehicle exhaust and Saharan dust transport

analogue_current.note: Caribbean tropical savanna climate with a comparable dry winter.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter, more humid Caribbean coastal conditions with a shorter dry season.

urban_fact: Habana Vieja’s dense colonial street grid wraps a narrow harbor entrance, linked by the Malecón seawall to mid-century Vedado and the sprawling, car-scarce suburbs built after the 1959 revolution froze much private development.
educational_debrief: Decades of limited private investment left Havana’s historic core largely intact rather than redeveloped, making it one of the best-preserved colonial Spanish port cities in the Americas despite chronic infrastructure decay.
cryptic_clue: Chrome-finned American cars from the 1950s still rumble down its streets, kept running for decades under a U.S. trade embargo that cut off new imports entirely. Its cigars are rolled a few blocks from the house where a Nobel-winning novelist spent two decades writing of an old fisherman and the sea.
image_caption: Skyline of Havana, Cuba, seen from the Vedado district

name: Guatemala City
peak_smog_season: Dry season agricultural burning haze and valley traffic inversion

analogue_current.note: Central American highland climate with mild, near-constant temperatures.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer highland-subtropical conditions as the dry season intensifies.

urban_fact: Built across a dissected highland plateau, Guatemala City is cut by deep ravines (barrancos) that host informal settlements and constrain east–west travel, with the formal city organized into numbered zonas since relocating here in 1776.
educational_debrief: Guatemala’s capital moved to its current highland valley site in 1776 after earthquakes destroyed the previous colonial capital at Antigua, and its barranco ravines remain both a housing refuge and a major landslide hazard today.
cryptic_clue: A scaled-down iron replica of a famous Parisian tower rises over its skyline, raised in 1935 to honor a 19th-century reformist president. Set on a highland plateau over 1,500 meters up — the highest of any capital on its isthmus — it's also that isthmus's single most populous metropolis.
image_caption: Aerial view of the high-rise skyline in Zone 14, Guatemala City

name: Brasília
peak_smog_season: Dry season (Aug–Sep) cerrado wildfire smoke

analogue_current.note: Central Brazilian cerrado savanna climate with the same sharp dry season.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter cerrado gateway conditions with an even longer dry season.

urban_fact: Lúcio Costa’s 1957 Plano Piloto forms an airplane-like silhouette, with a monumental government axis crossing curved residential ‘wings’ of superquadra blocks, the whole plan wrapped by the artificial Lake Paranoá.
educational_debrief: Inaugurated in 1960 to shift Brazil’s center of gravity inland from the crowded coast, Brasília is the paramount built example of Modernist urban planning and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, though its car-centric design famously under-served pedestrians.
cryptic_clue: A president promised '50 years of progress in five' and delivered, raising a capital from an empty red-dirt plateau in just 41 months. Its architect's sweeping white-concrete cathedral and twin bowl-shaped congress towers are instantly recognizable — a capital so young it earned UNESCO World Heritage status within his own lifetime.
image_caption: The National Congress Palace, Oscar Niemeyer's modernist landmark in Brasília
image_author: Edilson Rodrigues / Agência Senado via Wikimedia Commons

name: Caracas
peak_smog_season: Dry season valley temperature inversion trapping traffic emissions

analogue_current.note: Tropical highland-valley climate moderated by comparable elevation.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, more humid tropical conditions with heavier year-round rainfall.

urban_fact: Caracas fills a narrow, mountain-walled valley separated from the Caribbean coast by the Ávila range, with formal high-rise districts along the valley floor and vast informal barrios climbing the surrounding steep slopes.
educational_debrief: Oil-boom wealth built Caracas’s modernist valley-floor core in the mid-20th century, while subsequent rural-to-urban migration pushed informal self-built barrios up the steep surrounding hillsides, a divide still visible today.
cryptic_clue: Birthplace of the general who liberated half a continent from a single colonial crown, his name now stamped on currencies, plazas, and an entire nation renamed in his honor. Its international airport sits down on the coast, reached from downtown only by a hair-raising switchback highway through the mountains between them.
image_caption: Panoramic aerial view of Caracas, Venezuela

name: Manaus
peak_smog_season: Dry season (Aug–Sep) regional deforestation and wildfire smoke

analogue_current.note: Amazon rainforest river-port climate with a near-identical wet regime.

analogue_2050.note: Drier Amazonian conditions reflecting a longer, more pronounced dry season.

urban_fact: An Amazon River port reachable only by boat or plane, Manaus sits where the dark Rio Negro meets the sandy Solimões at the ‘Meeting of Waters,’ its Free Trade Zone economy isolated within the surrounding rainforest.
educational_debrief: No highway connects Manaus to Brazil’s main road network, so its Zona Franca industrial economy depends entirely on river barges and air freight, making it one of the world’s largest cities effectively isolated by terrain.
cryptic_clue: Rubber barons here grew so wealthy they shipped Italian marble and French ironwork thousands of kilometers upriver just to build a full opera house deep in the rainforest — inaugurated in 1896 with a touring European opera company, and it still stages full seasons today.
image_caption: Downtown skyline of Manaus, Amazonas, seen from Sumaúma Park Shopping

name: Santiago
peak_smog_season: Winter (Jun–Aug) thermal inversion trapping vehicle and wood-stove smoke in the Andean basin

analogue_current.note: Andean rain-shadow basin climate with a similarly dry, cool profile.

analogue_2050.note: Increasingly arid Central Valley conditions under intensifying drought.

urban_fact: Santiago fills a broad basin between the high Andes and the lower Chilean Coastal Range, split by the Mapocho River, with winter temperature inversions trapping smog against the surrounding mountain walls.
educational_debrief: Central Chile’s ongoing ‘megadrought,’ underway since 2010, has cut Santiago’s reservoir inflows dramatically and is among the most cited real-world examples of a dry Mediterranean-type climate aridifying under sustained warming.
cryptic_clue: A funicular climbs a hill in the middle of downtown, crowned by a giant white Madonna statue visible from nearly everywhere below. World-class ski slopes lie under two hours up one valley road; ripe vineyards, a similar drive down the other.
image_caption: The Sanhattan business district skyline with the Andes behind, Santiago, Chile

name: La Paz
peak_smog_season: Dry season (May–Aug) thermal inversion trapping vehicle exhaust in the canyon bowl

analogue_current.note: High-altitude Andean plateau climate with comparably mild, stable temperatures.

analogue_2050.note: Slightly warmer high-Andean conditions with reduced glacier-fed water supply.

urban_fact: La Paz plunges into a dramatic canyon carved by the Choqueyapu River below the Altiplano, with wealth inverted from most cities — the cold, high rim of El Alto is the poorest district, while the warmer canyon floor is the wealthiest.
educational_debrief: Retreating Andean glaciers that once buffered La Paz and El Alto’s dry-season water supply triggered a severe 2016 water crisis, and the metropolis now relies on the world’s largest urban cable-car network to link its steep, layered terrain.
cryptic_clue: The world's highest seat of government, though a different city keeps the constitutional title on paper. Market stalls blocks from the presidential palace sell dried llama fetuses, buried under new buildings for luck — a short ride from the vast high-altitude lake this stretch of mountains shares with a neighboring country.
image_caption: Panoramic view of central La Paz, the seat of government of Bolivia

name: Guangzhou
peak_smog_season: Summer photochemical ozone & winter Pearl River Delta regional haze

analogue_current.note: South China monsoon-humid-subtropical coastal climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, more tropical-trending subtropical conditions.

urban_fact: Guangzhou was for centuries the only Chinese port open to Europeans under the restrictive Canton System, and today anchors the Pearl River Delta megaregion along the historic foreign-trade waterfront.
educational_debrief: Guangzhou anchors the Pearl River Delta, one of the world's most densely built megaregions, where its urban footprint runs almost continuously into Shenzhen, Dongguan, and Hong Kong across the estuary. Sitting low and flat on the delta, the city faces recurring exposure to summer typhoons, storm surge, and monsoon flooding, which shapes ongoing drainage and coastal-defense planning. It has hosted the Canton Fair, one of the world's oldest and largest trade exhibitions, twice yearly since the 1950s, a modern echo of its centuries as China's principal port for foreign trade.
cryptic_clue: Known to old Western traders by an entirely different name — one still used today for its language and its cuisine — this river-delta city traces its founding to a legend of five rams sent by the gods bearing grain, memorialized in stone downtown. Its tradition of small steamed dishes over morning tea has gone global as shorthand for the whole regional cooking style.
image_caption: Huacheng Square and the Zhujiang New Town skyline, Guangzhou, China
image_author: Guangzhou Private Tours by Janvi via Wikimedia Commons

name: Shenzhen
peak_smog_season: Summer typhoon-season humidity & autumn regional haze

analogue_current.note: Adjacent Pearl River Delta monsoon-subtropical coastal climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, wetter tropical conditions year-round.

urban_fact: A fishing village of roughly 30,000 people in 1979, Shenzhen became China’s first Special Economic Zone in 1980 and grew into a migrant-driven tech and finance hub headquartering Huawei, Tencent, and DJI.
educational_debrief: Shenzhen is one of the most compressed urbanization stories on record: what was farmland and fishing villages in the late 1970s grew, within a single generation, into a metropolis of well over ten million people through its status as China's first and most successful Special Economic Zone. Wedged into a coastal bay bordering Hong Kong, the city's low-lying, densely built terrain leaves it exposed to typhoon storm surge and heavy monsoon rainfall, prompting significant investment in flood defenses and drainage as the delta warms. Its population remains disproportionately young and migrant-heavy relative to older Chinese cities, a legacy of decades of labor drawn in by its manufacturing and now technology sectors.
cryptic_clue: A single river marks the border with a former British colony next door, crossed by one of the busiest land checkpoints on Earth. A giant roadside portrait of the reformist leader who picked this stretch of coast for the country's boldest economic experiment still watches over the boulevard named for him.
image_caption: Modern skyline in the Longhua District of Shenzhen, China

name: Chongqing
peak_smog_season: Winter valley fog-trapped haze & summer stagnant furnace heat

analogue_current.note: Upper Yangtze River humid-subtropical basin climate.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified summer "furnace city" heat extremes.

urban_fact: A genuinely vertical "mountain city" at the confluence of the Yangtze and Jialing rivers, Chongqing stacks buildings and roads across elevations linked by cable cars and escalators, earning it the nickname "Fog City."
educational_debrief: Chongqing's mountainous, river-carved terrain makes it one of the least sprawl-friendly major cities anywhere: rather than spreading outward, it has built vertically, stacking roads, subway lines, and buildings across many different elevations linked by escalators, funiculars, and cable cars. Frequent temperature inversions trap humidity and haze over the Yangtze-Jialing confluence, reinforcing its long-standing nickname as one of China's so-called 'Fog Cities,' alongside Wuhan and Nanjing. As a directly administered municipality rather than a conventional city, its official population figures cover a metropolitan area unusually large in land area, encompassing many rural and semi-rural counties around the dense urban core.
cryptic_clue: When invaders took the coast, the wartime government retreated deep into these hills and endured years of relentless bombing without falling. Punishingly spicy hotpot, said to be invented by riverside dockworkers keeping warm and disguising cheap cuts of meat, is now its most famous export — administratively, it's the single most populous city-level division in the country.
image_caption: Cityscape of Chongqing, China, along the Yangtze/Jialing confluence
image_author: メイド理世 via Wikimedia Commons

name: Chengdu
peak_smog_season: Winter Sichuan Basin temperature-inversion haze

analogue_current.note: Sichuan Basin monsoon-humid-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, wetter subtropical basin conditions.

urban_fact: The only major Chinese city to keep an unchanged location and name across imperial, republican, and communist eras, Chengdu pairs giant-panda conservation fame with a "park city" planning push for green, walkable ring roads.
educational_debrief: Chengdu sprawls outward in concentric ring roads from an ancient core, a radial pattern planners are now trying to counterbalance with a 'park city' push for greenways and walkable districts rather than continuous outward sprawl. Sitting in the enclosed Sichuan Basin, the city experiences frequent haze and temperature inversions that trap pollution close to the ground, a recurring challenge distinct from coastal Chinese cities with better natural ventilation. It has kept the same name and roughly the same location for well over two thousand years, one of the longest continuous urban identities in East Asia.
cryptic_clue: A Tang-dynasty poet's thatched cottage still draws pilgrims here, beside a river once so vital to a booming silk-brocade trade that the city took its old nickname straight from the fabric. The black-and-white bears bred and shown off a short drive away have become the country's softest kind of ambassador.
image_caption: Central Chengdu skyline at dawn, Sichuan, China

name: Wuhan
peak_smog_season: Summer high-humidity heat & winter regional industrial haze

analogue_current.note: Middle Yangtze River humid-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified subtropical summer heat and humidity.

urban_fact: Historically three merged cities — Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang — at the confluence of the Han and Yangtze rivers, Wuhan grew into a major industrial and university hub still legible as distinct historic downtowns.
educational_debrief: Wuhan grew from three once-separate cities — Wuchang, Hankou, and Hanyang — that merged into a single metropolis straddling the confluence of the Yangtze and Han rivers, and its urban core still reads as three distinct historic downtowns linked by bridges and ferries. Its position directly on the Yangtze has long made it one of China's most flood-exposed major cities, with serious summer floods recurring through the twentieth century before large-scale flood-control investment in recent decades. Today it anchors a university-dense metropolitan area at the rail and river crossroads of central China, a centrality that made it an early target for industrial development.
cryptic_clue: A 1911 military uprising here lit the fuse that toppled over two thousand years of imperial rule within months. Its edge holds a lake so large it's said to be the biggest found entirely within any city's limits nationwide, and each spring its most famous university draws crowds for a hillside blanketed in cherry blossoms.
image_caption: View of the Wuhan skyline from the East Lake Greenway, China

name: Tianjin
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating thermal inversion & spring Gobi dust storms

analogue_current.note: North China Plain monsoon-continental climate.

analogue_2050.note: Drying semi-arid trend under continued warming.

urban_fact: A treaty port after 1858, Tianjin hosted nine foreign concessions whose European-style architecture still lines the Hai River, while a second modern core has grown since 1994 at the coastal Binhai New Area.
educational_debrief: Tianjin has grown as two distinct urban cores: the historic riverfront city shaped by its nineteenth-century treaty-port era, and the newer Binhai New Area built up along the coast since the 1990s as a separate deep-water port and industrial zone. Sitting barely above sea level near the river mouth, it faces meaningful coastal flood exposure, and projections point to it facing some of North China's most acute water stress by 2050 as groundwater and rainfall pressures intensify across the region. Its climate is also projected to trend drier and more semi-arid by mid-century, part of a broader aridification pattern expected across parts of the North China Plain.
cryptic_clue: The nearest seaport to a landlocked capital roughly 70 miles inland, this river city's colonial-era quarter left behind a full, walkable slice of Italy — the only authentic Italian-style town built outside Italy itself. A giant Ferris wheel today straddles the river directly on top of a highway bridge, a design found nowhere else on Earth.
image_caption: Urban skyline of Tianjin, China

name: Xi'an
peak_smog_season: Winter Guanzhong Plain temperature-inversion haze & spring dust

analogue_current.note: Ancient-capital inland climate at the subtropical-continental transition.

analogue_2050.note: Drier continental conditions further inland.

urban_fact: Capital of ancient Chang’an for a succession of dynasties and the Silk Road’s eastern terminus, Xi’an keeps its 1370 Ming-dynasty city wall — an 11.9km circuit that still defines the old city’s grid.
educational_debrief: During the Tang dynasty, Xi'an — then called Chang'an — is widely considered by historians to have been the largest and most cosmopolitan city in the world, a planned capital whose strict symmetrical grid of walled wards later served as a direct model for early Japanese capitals like Nara and Kyoto. The surviving Ming-dynasty city wall, an 11.9-kilometer rectangular circuit built centuries after Chang'an's peak, still defines the boundaries and grid orientation of Xi'an's old city today. As the eastern terminus of the Silk Road, the city built its historic wealth on overland trade with Central Asia and beyond, a role that faded as maritime trade routes came to dominate global commerce in later centuries.
cryptic_clue: Farmers digging a well in 1974 struck a buried army — thousands of life-sized clay soldiers guarding history's self-proclaimed 'First Emperor,' still sealed inside his unopened tomb. A pagoda across town once held the scriptures a monk hauled back from India, a real journey later reimagined as a tale of a mischievous monkey king.
image_caption: Skyline of Xi'an's central business district, Shaanxi, China

name: Nanjing
peak_smog_season: Summer furnace-city heat & winter regional industrial haze

analogue_current.note: Lower Yangtze Delta humid-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter subtropical summers further up the Yangtze basin.

urban_fact: Capital of the early Ming dynasty and later the Republic of China, Nanjing preserves the world’s longest surviving city-wall circuit alongside a historic palace and tomb complex on the Yangtze.
educational_debrief: Nanjing sits on the lower Yangtze in a humid subtropical climate long associated, alongside Chongqing and Wuhan, with China's so-called 'Furnace Cities' for its intense, muggy summer heat. Its urban form runs along the river in a linear pattern, with the historic walled city, Ming-era palace ruins, and newer development threading between hills and water rather than spreading in a uniform ring. Having served as capital under several dynasties and again as the Republic of China's capital before 1949, it retains an unusually dense concentration of imperial and republican-era heritage sites for a city of its size.
cryptic_clue: When the foreign engineers who'd helped build the first bridge across this same great river withdrew, this downstream capital built its own crossing anyway — the first the country ever engineered entirely by itself, a lasting point of national pride. A mausoleum on a nearby purple mountain honors the revolutionary remembered as the father of the modern republic.
image_caption: Nanjing skyline viewed across Xuanwu Lake, Jiangsu, China

name: Hangzhou
peak_smog_season: Summer high-humidity ozone & winter regional haze

analogue_current.note: Yangtze River Delta subtropical marine climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, more intense subtropical summer conditions.

urban_fact: Capital of the Southern Song dynasty when it was reputedly the world’s largest city, Hangzhou has been shaped ever since by UNESCO-listed West Lake, and today headquarters Alibaba and Ant Group.
educational_debrief: Hangzhou's urban form radiates outward in rings from West Lake, a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape that has shaped city planning and height restrictions in its historic core for centuries. Its economy has shifted dramatically in the twenty-first century from silk and tea trade toward technology and e-commerce, anchored by Alibaba and Ant Group, drawing a wave of young, highly educated migrants into a metro area that was already one of the wealthiest per-capita in China. Though not directly on the open coast, it sits near Hangzhou Bay and faces moderate coastal flood exposure alongside the broader water-management challenges typical of the Yangtze Delta.
cryptic_clue: Locals have ranked ten official "scenes" along its lake for eight centuries — one of them, three small stone pagodas rising from still water, appears on the country's own paper currency. The hills above grow a green tea so prized it once counted as imperial tribute.
image_caption: West Lake and the Hangzhou skyline, Zhejiang, China

name: Kunming
peak_smog_season: Dry-season agricultural burning haze (Feb-Apr)

analogue_current.note: Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau subtropical highland climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer highland tropical conditions.

urban_fact: Nicknamed the "City of Eternal Spring" for its narrow, mild year-round temperature range beside Dian Lake, Kunming has long served as China’s plateau gateway to Southeast Asia via the historic Tea Horse Road.
educational_debrief: Kunming's high elevation on the Yunnan-Guizhou Plateau gives it a subtropical highland climate with an unusually narrow temperature range across the year, rare for a Chinese city at this latitude and the source of its 'City of Eternal Spring' nickname. Despite sitting beside Dian Lake, the city faces high projected water stress by 2050, a combination of plateau geography, growing demand, and decades of pollution that have degraded the lake as a reliable water source. Long a gateway city linking China's interior to Southeast Asia via the historic Tea Horse Road, it has grown into a regional hub for trade and transport toward Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar.
cryptic_clue: Spring never quite leaves this plateau town, the seasons barely shifting from January to July. Just outside it, a forest grew from limestone instead of wood, rain and time carving its karst spires into needle-thin blades.
image_caption: Kunming skyline at sunset, Yunnan, China

name: Datong
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating smog in a historic coal-mining region

analogue_current.note: Cold semi-arid loess and steppe-plateau climate.

analogue_2050.note: Drier, hotter semi-arid conditions further west.

urban_fact: Capital of the Northern Wei dynasty and home to the UNESCO-listed Yungang Grottoes’ 50,000 carved Buddhist statues, Datong later became a major coal-mining center on the Shanxi loess plateau.
educational_debrief: Datong sits on the arid Shanxi loess plateau in a cold, semi-arid climate that leaves it facing high projected water stress by 2050, a common story across North China's coal belt. Long dependent on coal mining and coal-fired power, which brought both economic weight and some of China's worst historical air-quality problems, the city has more recently become a visible site for utility-scale solar power projects as the region works to diversify its energy base. Its grid-planned old town, walled and centered on its dynastic and Buddhist heritage, sits within a much larger municipal footprint still shaped by mining infrastructure.
cryptic_clue: A monastery clings to a cliff face nearby, its halls suspended on wooden pillars for close to 1,500 years. Below ground, the black seams this city was built on have kept furnaces lit across the country for generations.
image_caption: Aerial view of the old city skyline near the south gate, Datong, Shanxi, China

name: Changchun
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating smog & spring dust storms

analogue_current.note: Northeast China Manchurian continental climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer continental summers, milder winters.

urban_fact: Planned as "Hsinking," capital of Japan’s Manchukuo puppet state (1932-1945), Changchun kept wide colonial boulevards and greenery, then became China’s automotive hub via FAW, the "Detroit of China."
educational_debrief: Changchun's wide, tree-lined boulevards and radial street plan date to its years as 'Hsinking,' the purpose-built capital of Japan's Manchukuo puppet state, giving it an unusually planned, spacious layout compared with many older Chinese cities. Its cold, monsoon-influenced continental climate brings long, harsh winters and a short growing season, typical of Manchuria's interior latitude. The city's economy remains heavily concentrated around FAW and the broader automotive sector, a specialization that has powered growth but also leaves it more exposed than diversified metro areas to shifts in the industry.
cryptic_clue: Its name literally translates to "long spring," though the season it's actually known for is a brutal Manchurian winter. Behind its wide, tree-lined boulevards sits the country's first major film studio, opened in 1945 and still called the cradle of its cinema today.
image_caption: Changchun skyline with the Ji Tower, Jilin, China

name: Harbin
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating smog during the extreme-cold season

analogue_current.note: Far-northeast Manchurian continental climate.

analogue_2050.note: Milder, coastally moderated Northeast China winters.

urban_fact: Founded in 1898 as a hub of the Russian-built Chinese Eastern Railway, Harbin kept a cosmopolitan Russian heritage visible in the Saint Sophia Cathedral, and now turns its extreme cold into the Ice and Snow Sculpture Festival.
educational_debrief: Harbin's winters are among the coldest of any major city on Earth, a severity that shapes everything from building heating standards to the city's identity around ice and snow tourism. Its built-up area follows the Songhua River in a linear band, with the historic Russian-influenced core near the water and newer districts extending along the transportation corridors the railway first established. As the historic terminus of the Russian-built Chinese Eastern Railway, it became one of the most cosmopolitan cities in early twentieth-century Asia, a legacy still visible in its street grid and surviving Orthodox architecture.
cryptic_clue: Onion domes still crown its skyline, a leftover from a railway-building empire that collapsed a century ago, in one of the coldest big cities anywhere on the map. A local brewery, older than the republic itself, has been warming stomachs since 1900.
image_caption: Cityscape view of Harbin, Heilongjiang province, China

name: Shenyang
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating inversion across this former rust-belt industrial city

analogue_current.note: Liaoning industrial-belt continental climate.

analogue_2050.note: Milder, coastally moderated border-city winters.

urban_fact: Political center of the rising Manchu state after 1625, when Nurhaci built the Mukden Palace, Shenyang became a major heavy-industry hub under Japanese occupation and later a symbol of China’s industrial "rust belt."
educational_debrief: Shenyang anchors China's historic 'rust belt,' having grown into one of the country's largest heavy-industry and machinery-manufacturing centers under Japanese occupation and through the socialist planned-economy era, a legacy that brought both scale and, later, painful state-enterprise restructuring from the 1990s onward. Its radial street pattern grew outward from the Manchu-era Mukden Palace core, expanding through successive waves of industrial development. Sitting inland in a continental climate zone, it faces high projected water stress by 2050, part of a broader pattern across China's northeastern industrial cities.
cryptic_clue: A pocket-sized cousin of the nation's Forbidden City rises here, built by a rising dynasty before it ever took the bigger throne. Decades later, a staged railway explosion in this same city gave an invading army its pretext for war.
image_caption: Skyline of the Tiexi district in Shenyang, China

name: Xiamen
peak_smog_season: Summer typhoon-season humidity & occasional regional haze intrusions

analogue_current.note: Coastal Fujian monsoon-humid-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, more tropical-trending coastal conditions.

urban_fact: A fortified port grown into one of Deng Xiaoping’s original Special Economic Zones, Xiamen pairs a high-rise SEZ core with the offshore islet Gulangyu, whose dense Victorian-era colonial architecture is UNESCO-listed.
educational_debrief: Xiamen's island-and-archipelago geography, split across a mainland core and offshore islets including car-free Gulangyu, has produced a more compact, ferry-linked urban form than most mainland Chinese Special Economic Zones. Its low-lying coastal position leaves it highly exposed to typhoon landfall and storm surge each summer and autumn, a recurring risk along this stretch of the Taiwan Strait coast. Since becoming one of Deng Xiaoping's original 1980s Special Economic Zones, it has grown from a modest port town into a wealthier, more service- and trade-oriented economy than many of its faster-industrializing SEZ peers.
cryptic_clue: An islet just offshore bans cars outright and packs in more pianos per resident than anywhere else in the country, a leftover from missionary schools and old foreign concessions. Traders once knew the whole port by a different name entirely, the one that stuck on Western maps for a century.
image_caption: Xiamen skyline at night, seen from Gulangyu Island

name: Qiqihar
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating smog in this heavy-equipment manufacturing city

analogue_current.note: Northeast China plain continental climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer continental summers under continued warming.

urban_fact: A railway junction after the 1903 Chinese Eastern Railway and a Soviet-aided heavy-equipment manufacturing center from the 1950s, Qiqihar sits beside the Zhalong wetlands, a key breeding ground for the red-crowned crane.
educational_debrief: Qiqihar sits beside the Zhalong wetlands, one of Northeast Asia's most important breeding grounds for the endangered red-crowned crane and a rare large freshwater marsh ecosystem this far north in a heavily industrialized region. Like many of China's smaller northeastern rust-belt cities, its population and economic growth have lagged the booming coastal metros in recent decades, even as its Soviet-era heavy-machinery industry remains a significant local employer. Its cold, monsoon-influenced continental climate brings a short growing season and long winters typical of Heilongjiang province.
cryptic_clue: Marshland at the edge of town shelters one of the last strongholds of a crane so revered in local myth it stands for a thousand years of luck. The city itself grew up around a rail junction, later turning out the heavy machinery that powered a young nation's industrial push.
image_caption: Qiqihar skyline photographed from Longsha Park

name: Osaka
peak_smog_season: Summer high-humidity photochemical ozone

analogue_current.note: Adjacent Kansai-region humid-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, more intense subtropical summer conditions.

urban_fact: Japan’s premier Edo-period merchant city, Osaka hosted the Dōjima Rice Exchange — widely cited as the world’s first organized futures market, founded in 1697 — and once had roughly 1,629 canal bridges.
educational_debrief: Long before Tokyo eclipsed it, Osaka was Edo-period Japan's commercial hub, where regional feudal domains shipped their rice to be sold and priced at the Dōjima exchange — a role that earned it the enduring nickname 'the nation's kitchen' even after political power concentrated in Tokyo. Built low and flat across a river delta opening onto Osaka Bay, the city experienced serious land subsidence through the mid-20th century from unchecked groundwater pumping for industry, a problem later brought under control through regulation. That same flat, reclaimed bay geography later enabled one of modern Japan's largest engineering projects, Kansai International Airport, built entirely on an artificial island offshore so it wouldn't have to disrupt the dense city on land.
cryptic_clue: Known for centuries as "the nation's kitchen," this merchant town still sizzles octopus dumplings on nearly every corner. Its castle, built by the general credited with unifying the country, sits behind a moat wide enough to swallow armies.
image_caption: Osaka skyline at night from the Umeda Sky Building observation deck

name: Nagoya
peak_smog_season: Summer high-humidity ozone & typhoon-season heavy rain

analogue_current.note: Pacific coast Japanese humid-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer subtropical conditions further west.

urban_fact: Rebuilt on a deliberately orderly grid after WWII around its 1610 castle town, Nagoya anchors Japan’s automotive manufacturing heartland — Toyota is headquartered in greater Nagoya (Aichi Prefecture).
educational_debrief: Nagoya anchors Japan's Chubu manufacturing corridor, the industrial base centered on Toyota and its supplier network that has made greater Nagoya one of the country's most export-oriented regional economies. Positioned midway between Tokyo and Osaka along the Tokaido corridor, it has long functioned as a transport and logistics hinge for central Japan's rail and highway networks. Its low-lying position on Ise Bay leaves parts of the city exposed to storm-surge flooding, a risk that shaped its systematic postwar rebuilding around wide, fire-break boulevards radiating from the reconstructed castle-town core.
cryptic_clue: A shrine here is said to guard one of the three sacred treasures of the imperial throne, a legendary sword pulled from a serpent's tail in myth. Above the nearby castle, a pair of gold dolphin-fish ornaments have watched over the skyline since the age of shoguns.
image_caption: Skyline of Nagoya, Japan

name: Sapporo
peak_smog_season: Rare — mild spring pollen haze in an otherwise clean-air city

analogue_current.note: Hokkaido cold humid-continental climate.

analogue_2050.note: Milder, coastally moderated Hokkaido winters.

urban_fact: Laid out on a strict Western-style grid when Japan’s Meiji government founded the Hokkaido Development Commission there in 1869, Sapporo hosted Asia’s first Winter Olympics in 1972 and draws millions to its Snow Festival.
educational_debrief: Sapporo is one of the snowiest major cities in the world, accumulating heavy snowfall most winters, a climate reality that shaped both its Meiji-era Western-style street grid, built wide enough for snow clearance, and its economy around winter sports and tourism. As Hokkaido's capital and by far Japan's youngest large city, having been essentially founded rather than inherited from a castle-town past, it lacks the medieval urban layers common elsewhere in Japan. Its relatively low coastal flood risk and water stress, compared with many Japanese metros, reflect Hokkaido's cooler climate and lower population density even as the island faces distinct seasonal challenges of its own.
cryptic_clue: An American agricultural advisor's parting words to his students here — "boys, be ambitious" — got cast into a statue that's now a civic icon. The beer brand born in that same frontier era still wears a red star on every bottle.
image_caption: Sapporo skyline, Hokkaido, Japan

name: Sendai
peak_smog_season: Minimal regional haze; rare spring pollen episodes

analogue_current.note: Honshu regional humid-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer subtropical-trending regional summers.

urban_fact: Founded as a 1600 castle town by daimyo Date Masamune, Sendai is nicknamed the "City of Trees" for its zelkova-lined boulevards, and its port was closed for weeks after the devastating March 2011 tsunami.
educational_debrief: Sendai carries an extremely high coastal flood risk, reflecting both its exposed Pacific coastline and the catastrophic 2011 Tohoku earthquake and tsunami, after which the city rebuilt substantial stretches of coastal defense and relocated some vulnerable neighborhoods further inland. As the largest city in the Tohoku region, it functions as the area's administrative, commercial, and transport hub, drawing population from a much more rural surrounding hinterland. Its zelkova-lined boulevards, replanted after wartime destruction, give the city one of the higher tree canopies among dense Japanese urban cores.
cryptic_clue: A one-eyed warlord nicknamed "the Dragon" founded this castle town, and his crescent-moon helmet remains one of the most recognizable in the country's history. Every August, its main streets vanish under enormous paper streamers for one of the nation's largest star festivals.
image_caption: Sendai skyline and the Hirose River seen from Hyojogawara Bridge

name: Naha
peak_smog_season: Typhoon-season heavy rain rather than smog; mild trade-wind haze

analogue_current.note: Southern Kyushu warm-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, tropical-trending southern Okinawan islands.

urban_fact: Former port capital of the independent Ryukyu Kingdom, Naha centers on Shuri Castle, a UNESCO gusuku site almost entirely destroyed in the 1945 Battle of Okinawa and since substantially reconstructed.
educational_debrief: Naha's projected shift from a humid subtropical to a tropical monsoon climate classification by 2050 reflects Okinawa's position at the warm southern edge of Japan, already closer in climate to Taiwan and the northern Philippines than to Tokyo. Built on a compact coastal footprint with little room to spread across its small island setting, the city carries an extremely high coastal flood risk rating, compounding its exposure to typhoons that regularly track through the Ryukyu chain. Its culture, cuisine, and until-recent traffic patterns remain distinct from mainland Japan, a legacy of the centuries it spent as an independent trading kingdom before its 1879 annexation.
cryptic_clue: This port once ruled its own independent kingdom until an 1879 annexation folded it into a larger nation. It kept driving on the opposite side of the road from the rest of that nation for decades after, switching overnight in a single 1978 operation.
image_caption: Panorama of Naha City and its surroundings from Shuri Castle

name: Busan
peak_smog_season: Spring Asian dust (hwangsa) & winter transboundary particulates

analogue_current.note: Southeastern Korean coastal humid-subtropical climate.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer maritime subtropical-trending conditions.

urban_fact: South Korea’s busiest port and the world’s sixth-largest container port, Busan is squeezed into narrow valleys between mountains and the sea, and served as the country’s de facto wartime capital in 1950-53.
educational_debrief: Busan's urban form is squeezed into narrow valleys between steep coastal mountains and the sea, producing a famously compact, vertically stacked cityscape with limited room for conventional outward sprawl. Its population swelled rapidly during the 1950-53 Korean War, when it served as the country's provisional capital and absorbed a large wave of refugees from the north, a demographic surge still visible in some of its older hillside neighborhoods. As South Korea's principal port, its economy remains deeply tied to shipping and container throughput, complemented in recent decades by a growing film and cultural-festival industry.
cryptic_clue: Every autumn, red carpets roll out here for one of Asia's biggest film festivals. The same port is just as well known for a rainbow-colored hillside village of stacked houses, built by refugees who had nowhere else to go during a war on the peninsula.
image_caption: Busan Cinema Center and the Centum City skyline at night
image_author: Raja Syazwina RS via Wikimedia Commons

name: Daegu
peak_smog_season: Summer basin-trapped heat & spring Asian dust (hwangsa)

analogue_current.note: Inland South Korean monsoon-humid-subtropical basin climate.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter inland basin summer extremes.

urban_fact: Sitting in a mountain-ringed basin that traps heat, Daegu produces South Korea’s most extreme urban summer heat island — locally nicknamed "Daefrica" — after decades as the country’s textile-manufacturing center.
educational_debrief: Daegu sits in a mountain-ringed river basin that traps heat and limits airflow, producing South Korea's most extreme urban heat-island effect and the local nickname 'Daefrica' for its punishing summers. That same enclosed basin geography, combined with growing demand, has left it facing higher projected water stress by 2050 than most other major Korean cities. Once the country's dominant textile-manufacturing center, it has spent recent decades diversifying toward medical technology and other advanced manufacturing as textile production declined domestically.
cryptic_clue: A mountain temple nearby has sheltered over 80,000 carved wooden printing blocks of a Buddhist scripture for close to 800 years, preserved by ventilation nobody's fully explained since. The basin city below built its fortune on textile looms and, until warming pushed the orchards north, some of the country's finest apples.
image_caption: Nighttime cityscape of Daegu, South Korea

name: Lahore
peak_smog_season: Autumn/winter crop-stubble burning and temperature inversion (Nov–Jan smog season)

analogue_current.note: Shares a hot semi-arid subtropical rainfall regime with a short, intense monsoon peak.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, drier hot-desert conditions typical of the Indus plains under further aridification.

urban_fact: The Mughal-era Walled City and Lahore Fort anchor a core ringed by colonial cantonment districts that grew along canal and rail lines.
educational_debrief: Lahore was ranked the world’s most polluted city in 2022, and its Walled City and colonial cantonment layers now sit beneath a fast-growing Metrobus and metro network built to serve over 13 million residents.
cryptic_clue: A local saying insists this place is simply unlike anywhere else — practically a boast built into the local dialect. Its skyline holds one of the largest mosques the Mughals ever built, and a nearby UNESCO-listed garden still channels water through the same terraced pools laid out for a 17th-century emperor's pleasure.
image_caption: View over Lahore, Pakistan, from the Wazir Khan Mosque

name: Bangalore
peak_smog_season: Winter post-monsoon calm-wind stagnation and vehicular exhaust build-up

analogue_current.note: Warm, moderately elevated tropical savanna rainfall pattern with a pronounced wet season.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified tropical savanna heat and monsoon variability under further warming.

urban_fact: Historic market wards (pētes) sit at the core of a tech-driven sprawl across former lakebeds and IT corridors like Whitefield and Electronic City.
educational_debrief: Bangalore’s ‘Garden City’ lake network has shrunk from roughly 265 interconnected tanks to under 100, and its 2023–24 groundwater crisis shows how IT-driven sprawl can outpace water infrastructure even at a relatively temperate elevation.
cryptic_clue: Colonial officers once retreated here specifically for cooler, spring-like air at altitude, a relief from the plains below. That same climate edge helped turn it, a century later, into the country's answer to Silicon Valley — and, unofficially, its pub capital too.
image_caption: Bangalore (Bengaluru) skyline, India

name: Chennai
peak_smog_season: Winter post-monsoon calm-wind stagnation and vehicular exhaust build-up

analogue_current.note: Coromandel/east Indian coast dry-summer tropical savanna with a similar northeast-monsoon rainfall skew.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer coastal tropical climate with an intensified northeast monsoon.

urban_fact: Height restrictions near the port’s weather radar, lifted only around 2009, pushed the city to sprawl horizontally along the Coromandel Coast rather than upward.
educational_debrief: Chennai’s 2019 ‘Day Zero’ crisis, when reservoirs ran dry mid-year, showed how a single skewed northeast-monsoon season can threaten water supply for a coastal megacity of nearly nine million.
cryptic_clue: One of the world's longest urban beaches runs along this shore, while inland the first English fortress ever built in the country still stands from its East India Company days. Come December, its concert halls fill for a month-long classical music season locals treat like a second monsoon.
image_caption: Skyline of Chennai, India

name: Kolkata
peak_smog_season: Winter fog and post-Diwali firecracker/biomass burning smog

analogue_current.note: Ganges-Brahmaputra delta-adjacent tropical savanna with a heavy southwest-monsoon peak.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, wetter tropical conditions with an intensified summer monsoon.

urban_fact: British India’s former capital retains a dense 19th-century colonial core beside the Maidan, still served by one of Asia’s oldest running tram networks.
educational_debrief: Kolkata’s planned satellite townships east of the historic core, like Salt Lake City and New Town, were built specifically to relieve pressure on one of the world’s most densely populated urban cores.
cryptic_clue: A cantilever bridge over the river here carries some of the heaviest traffic of any bridge on the planet, riveted together without a single nut or bolt. Every autumn the whole place transforms for a goddess-worshipping festival so elaborate UNESCO now lists it as intangible heritage.
image_caption: Kolkata's central business district skyline, India

name: Hyderabad
peak_smog_season: Winter inversion and pre-monsoon construction dust

analogue_current.note: Deccan plateau tropical savanna bordering semi-arid, with a similar monsoon-concentrated rainy season.

analogue_2050.note: Hot semi-arid conditions with a shorter, more erratic monsoon.

urban_fact: The Qutb Shahi-era old city around Charminar and Golconda Fort sits on a granite landscape once dotted with 140-plus artificial lakes, including the large Hussain Sagar.
educational_debrief: Hyderabad’s post-1990s HITEC City IT corridor grew on the same granite plateau its Nizam-era rulers once covered with artificial lakes for water storage, layering a tech boom onto centuries-old water infrastructure.
cryptic_clue: Its last hereditary ruler was once considered the richest man alive, a fortune so vast the stories still get exaggerated. Locals still argue over the correct way to layer the rice-and-meat dish that made this place a culinary pilgrimage, sealed in dough and cooked low over slow coals.
image_caption: High-rise office towers lit up at night in Hyderabad's Hi-Tech City
image_author: Mohammad Anees Qamar via Wikimedia Commons

name: Pune
peak_smog_season: Winter temperature inversion with vehicular and construction particulate build-up

analogue_current.note: Western Deccan Plateau tropical savanna bordering semi-arid, moderated by elevation.

analogue_2050.note: Hot semi-arid climate with a shorter monsoon and hotter pre-monsoon months.

urban_fact: Eighteenth-century Peshwa-era peths form the old city core, while a separate British cantonment built after 1817 created a bifurcated old-town/cantonment layout.
educational_debrief: Pune’s shift from a bifurcated old-town/cantonment layout to a purpose-built tech and auto-manufacturing hub at Hinjawadi, Magarpatta, and Kharadi mirrors Lahore’s own colonial-cantonment urban DNA half a subcontinent away.
cryptic_clue: Sheltered in the rain shadow east of a great coastal range, this onetime seat of Maratha power built so many colleges it earned the nickname 'Oxford of the East.'
image_caption: Skyline of Pune, India, seen from Koregaon Park

name: Varanasi
peak_smog_season: Winter Indo-Gangetic Plain haze and crop-residue burning

analogue_current.note: Ganges-plain humid subtropical climate with a hot, dry pre-monsoon spring.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified pre-monsoon heat and a shorter, heavier monsoon burst.

urban_fact: One of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities, its roughly 88 stepped riverfront ghats line a crescent bend of the Ganges.
educational_debrief: Varanasi’s dense, narrow-laned old-city fabric threads between more than 3,300 religious sites, making conventional street-grid infrastructure and modern flood or heat-response planning unusually difficult to retrofit.
cryptic_clue: One of its own names translates to 'City of Light,' and an American writer once called it older than legend itself. A famous hand-loomed silk still carries an older version of its name.
image_caption: Ahilya Ghat on the Ganges river in Varanasi, India

name: Thiruvananthapuram
peak_smog_season: Pre-monsoon haze and coastal humidity trapping of traffic emissions

analogue_current.note: Kerala Arabian Sea coast tropical monsoon climate with a flat, narrow year-round temperature range.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer coastal monsoon conditions with heavier southwest-monsoon downpours.

urban_fact: Built across seven hills near India’s southern tip, the city pairs Technopark, India’s first dedicated IT park, with the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre.
educational_debrief: Thiruvananthapuram’s flat, narrow year-round temperature range — barely 2°C between its warmest and coolest months — is a textbook signature of a low-latitude coastal station shielded from continental extremes.
cryptic_clue: Named for the coiled serpent beneath a reclining god, its temple's sealed vaults turned out to hold one of the largest hoards of gold and jewels ever found — uncovered only in 2011.
image_caption: A golden-hour evening street scene in Thiruvananthapuram (Trivandrum), Kerala, India

name: Mysuru
peak_smog_season: Dry-season agricultural burning and vehicular dust in the pre-monsoon months

analogue_current.note: Deccan-adjacent tropical savanna with a comparable dry-and-wet seasonal split.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer elevated tropical savanna with a longer dry season.

urban_fact: One of the first cities in Asia to undergo formal, board-led planned development after 1903, giving Mysuru a wide-boulevard, heritage-preserved core.
educational_debrief: Mysuru’s early adoption of formal urban planning under the 1903 City Improvement Trust Board left it with an unusually low-density, heritage-preserved core compared to most Indian cities of similar size.
cryptic_clue: Named for a buffalo-demon slain by a goddess on the hill above it, this city strings roughly a hundred thousand bulbs across its palace each autumn for a ten-day festival.
image_caption: Front facade of the Mysore Palace (Amba Vilas) in Mysuru, India

name: Kabul
peak_smog_season: Winter temperature inversion trapped in the Kabul valley, worsened by low-grade coal/wood heating

analogue_current.note: High-elevation cold semi-arid basin climate with cold winters and low year-round precipitation.

analogue_2050.note: Drier, more desert-leaning semi-arid conditions under continued warming.

urban_fact: Ringed closely by mountains including Koh-e Asamai and Sher Darwaza, the city’s footprint is squeezed into a narrow Hindu Kush valley along the Kabul River.
educational_debrief: Kabul’s population grew from roughly 500,000 in 2001 to over 5 million today, layering Soviet-era microrayon blocks and post-2001 gated development onto a mountain-hemmed valley never built for this scale.
cryptic_clue: A conqueror who built an empire to its south chose not to be buried among its riches, but here, in a hillside garden he planted himself.
image_caption: View over the old city of Kabul, Afghanistan

name: Rajshahi
peak_smog_season: Winter dry-season particulate build-up, easing markedly after recent emissions reductions

analogue_current.note: Ganges-basin humid subtropical climate with a comparable dry-winter, monsoon-summer pattern.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer Gangetic-plain subtropical climate with an intensified summer monsoon.

urban_fact: Known as both the ‘Education City’ and ‘Silk City,’ Rajshahi sits on the north bank of the Padma River, the Bangladeshi channel of the Ganges.
educational_debrief: Rajshahi’s local transit runs mostly on electric and traditional rickshaws rather than a formal transit network, and the city posted one of the steepest air-quality improvements recorded worldwide over a recent two-year span.
cryptic_clue: Home to the country's oldest university outside its capital, this river city's summer mango harvest draws buyers from across the nation every June.
image_caption: Street-level urban scene in Rajshahi, Bangladesh

name: Colombo
peak_smog_season: Dry-season (Feb–Mar) haze from regional agricultural burning and traffic

analogue_current.note: Equatorial Indian Ocean tropical rainforest with year-round heavy, evenly distributed rainfall.

analogue_2050.note: Intensified equatorial rainfall and heat under continued warming.

urban_fact: Portuguese, Dutch, and British colonial periods each left distinct architecture concentrated in the historic Fort district and Pettah market quarter.
educational_debrief: Colombo’s Beira Lake and international port sit within a few blocks of a colonial core shaped by three successive European powers, a compressed layering of history unusual even among former colonial capitals.
cryptic_clue: Legend wrongly links its name to a European explorer who never actually sailed here; it really comes from a Sinhala phrase for a harbor lined with mango trees.
image_caption: Colombo city skyline at night with the Lotus Tower, Sri Lanka

name: Urumqi
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating inversion, with December often reaching very unhealthy levels

analogue_current.note: Xinjiang desert-basin cold desert climate with an extreme continental temperature swing.

analogue_2050.note: Even hotter, drier desert-basin conditions under continued warming.

urban_fact: Reputed to be the major city farthest from any ocean on Earth, Urumqi sits between the Gurbantünggüt and Taklamakan deserts at the foot of the Tianshan mountains.
educational_debrief: A Tang-dynasty Silk Road garrison town turned modern oil, gas, and petrochemical hub, Urumqi’s roughly 40°C swing between its coldest and warmest month means is among the most extreme continental temperature ranges in this entire pool.
cryptic_clue: Its name, borrowed from a Mongolic tongue, once meant 'beautiful pasture.' Today a red sandstone hill crowned by a pagoda watches over its skyline instead.
image_caption: Urumqi's central business district seen from Hong Shan, Xinjiang, China

name: Kashgar
peak_smog_season: Spring regional sandstorms, worst in March, compounded by industrial emissions

analogue_current.note: Tarim Basin oasis cold desert climate at comparable elevation and extreme aridity.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter Central Asian desert-oasis conditions under continued warming.

urban_fact: Among the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities, this Silk Road oasis centers on the Id Kah Mosque, one of China’s largest, and its traditional bazaar.
educational_debrief: Kashgar’s historic old town, still predominantly Uyghur, sits at the western edge of the Taklamakan Desert — a strategic oasis crossroads that linked China to Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe for over a thousand years.
cryptic_clue: Two branches of an ancient trade route — one hugging each rim of a forbidding desert — meet again at this oasis, where herders have filled a weekly livestock bazaar for centuries.
image_caption: Kashgar Old City, Xinjiang, China

name: Bishkek
peak_smog_season: Winter temperature-inversion smog typical of basin-ringed Central Asian capitals

analogue_current.note: Central Asian continental basin climate with a comparable spring-wet, summer-dry pattern.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer, drier semi-arid conditions typical of a warming Central Asian steppe.

urban_fact: Laid out on a strict Soviet-era grid with wide boulevards, the city is threaded by irrigation channels (‘aryks’) that water dense rows of shade trees.
educational_debrief: Bishkek’s aryk-irrigated street trees, a distinctive Soviet-era Central Asian planning signature, depend on Tian Shan snowmelt — Kyrgyzstan’s upstream ‘water tower’ position leaves it less water-stressed than downstream neighbors like Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan.
cryptic_clue: Named until 1991 for a Bolshevik general born within its walls, this capital reclaimed an older name some trace to the wooden churn used for fermenting mare's milk.
image_caption: Overview of the main downtown road in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan

name: Tashkent
peak_smog_season: Summer photochemical ozone and winter thermal inversion

analogue_current.note: Same Central Asian dry-summer continental Mediterranean rainfall cycle.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter, drier semi-arid conditions typical of the Kyzylkum desert margin.

urban_fact: Almost entirely rebuilt after a devastating 1966 earthquake into a model Soviet city of wide tree-lined boulevards, fountains, and monuments.
educational_debrief: Tashkent’s post-1966 reconstruction produced Central Asia’s first metro system, and the same Csa climate that makes it a close match for Madrid in this dataset is projected to drift toward hot semi-arid conditions by 2050, just as Madrid’s own is.
cryptic_clue: Its Turkic name translates simply to 'City of Stone.' It also holds one of the world's oldest surviving Quran manuscripts, safeguarded here since Soviet times.
image_caption: Skyline of Tashkent, Uzbekistan

name: Astana
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating season inversion, with January daily peaks up to 64 µg/m³

analogue_current.note: West Siberian steppe humid continental climate with comparably severe winters.

analogue_2050.note: Warmer-summer continental conditions typical of a warming Ural-steppe transition zone.

urban_fact: A purpose-built capital relocated from Almaty in 1997, its Ishim River divides an older northern quarter from a newer administrative showcase south masterplanned in part by Kisho Kurokawa and Norman Foster.
educational_debrief: The second-coldest national capital in the world after Ulaanbaatar, Astana’s entire modern skyline postdates its 1997 relocation from Almaty — a rare case of a capital city whose built form is almost entirely younger than 30 years.
cryptic_clue: This capital has worn at least five different names in under two centuries, most recently swapping a president's name back for one that just means 'capital.'
image_caption: Central downtown Astana looking toward the Ak Orda from the Bayterek tower, Kazakhstan
image_author: Ken and Nyetta via Wikimedia Commons

name: Dushanbe
peak_smog_season: Winter valley temperature inversion with significant day-to-day variability

analogue_current.note: Mountain-basin hot-summer Mediterranean climate with a dry, hot summer season.

analogue_2050.note: Hot semi-arid conditions with a shorter, drier rainy season.

urban_fact: Named for the Persian word for ‘Monday,’ reflecting its origin as a weekly bazaar town, roughly 80% of Dushanbe’s built-up area is confined to a narrow valley floor.
educational_debrief: Dushanbe sits in a high-seismicity zone capable of magnitude 7.5–8 earthquakes, a risk that has directly shaped building codes in a city where four-fifths of the urban footprint is squeezed onto an 18-to-100-kilometer-wide valley floor.
cryptic_clue: For a few years this capital held the record for the world's tallest flagpole, before flashier rivals in the Gulf built past it.
image_caption: Central Dushanbe, Tajikistan

name: Ashgabat
peak_smog_season: Summer Karakum Desert dust storms and heat-driven particulate suspension

analogue_current.note: Karakum Desert-margin cold desert climate with a comparable winter-spring rainfall peak.

analogue_2050.note: Hotter, drier desert conditions typical of the Amu Darya lowlands.

urban_fact: Rebuilt after a catastrophic 1948 earthquake, Ashgabat holds a Guinness World Record for the highest concentration of white marble buildings anywhere.
educational_debrief: Ashgabat’s showcase white-marble core sits between the Karakum Desert and the Köpetdag mountains, entirely dependent on the Soviet-era Karakum Canal for the water that keeps a desert capital of over a million people running.
cryptic_clue: Its name is often translated from Persian roots as 'city of love.' It once crowned a monument with a gold-leafed statue of a former president that slowly rotated to keep him always facing the sun.
image_caption: View of Ashgabat, the white-marble capital of Turkmenistan

name: Karaganda
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-mining and heating-season particulate build-up

analogue_current.note: Kazakh Uplands steppe humid continental climate with comparably severe, dry winters.

analogue_2050.note: Slightly warmer continental steppe conditions under further warming.

urban_fact: Karaganda exists because of coal: the city was built from scratch on open steppe in 1931 purely to mine it, and the water shortage that came with that site was never solved locally — even now, supply is imported over 400 km via the Irtysh–Karaganda Canal, completed in the 1960s.
educational_debrief: Karaganda’s water supply travels over 400 kilometers through the Soviet-era Irtysh–Karaganda Canal, a concrete signature of chronic scarcity in a steppe city whose coal-mining economy has contracted to just 8 operating mines from 26 in Soviet times.
cryptic_clue: Forced laborers and entire deported ethnic minorities built much of this steppe city, which lent its name to one of the Soviet Union's largest Gulag camp networks.
image_caption: Winter street scene in Karaganda, Kazakhstan

name: Novosibirsk
peak_smog_season: Winter wood/coal residential heating haze during temperature inversions

analogue_current.note: West Siberian humid continental climate with comparably severe, snowy winters.

analogue_2050.note: Slightly warmer continental summers typical of a warming West Siberian basin.

urban_fact: When the Trans-Siberian Railway needed to cross the Ob River in 1893, the settlement that grew up around that crossing became Novosibirsk, a city that today is also home to Akademgorodok, a dedicated Soviet-era science-city research complex.
educational_debrief: Novosibirsk grew from a single railway river-crossing into Siberia’s largest transport and industrial hub, and its Novosibirsk Metro, opened in 1985, remains the only metro system in Siberia.
cryptic_clue: Its own name literally just means 'New Siberian City' — yet in barely a century from its founding, it grew into its country's third-largest metropolis.
image_caption: Novosibirsk skyline in winter, Russia
image_author: Novosibirsk travel on Al-Ashraf via Wikimedia Commons

name: Yekaterinburg
peak_smog_season: Winter inversion with road-transport exhaust as the dominant source (80% of local pollution)

analogue_current.note: Ural-region humid continental climate with a comparable severe-winter, mild-summer profile.

analogue_2050.note: Slightly warmer continental summers typical of a warming Ural-Volga transition zone.

urban_fact: Constructivist architecture survives here in unusually large quantities, a Soviet-era layer built on top of a much older industrial foundation: Yekaterinburg began in 1723 as an iron-making center on the Asian side of the Ural Mountains.
educational_debrief: Renamed Sverdlovsk for most of the Soviet period before reverting to Yekaterinburg, the city where the Romanov imperial family was executed in 1918 now traces 80% of its air pollution to road transport rather than the heavy industry that built it.
cryptic_clue: Named for an empress consort, this city sits so close to the line separating two continents that a roadside obelisk just outside it lets visitors stand with one foot in each.
image_caption: Yekaterinburg skyline seen from the City Pond, Russia

name: Ulan-Ude
peak_smog_season: Winter coal and wood-stove heating smog, persistent through most of the cold season

analogue_current.note: Inner Asian steppe-continental climate with a comparably extreme dry-winter, wet-summer swing.

analogue_2050.note: Slightly warmer continental summers typical of a warming Inner Asian steppe.

urban_fact: Sitting at the confluence of the Selenga and Uda rivers near Lake Baikal, the city is Russia’s principal center of Tibetan Buddhism and home to a 7.7-metre, 42-tonne Lenin head.
educational_debrief: Ulan-Ude sits where the Trans-Siberian Railway meets the branch line toward Ulaanbaatar and Beijing, and its razor-thin annual precipitation — barely a tenth of Colombo’s — comes almost entirely in a single summer wet season.
cryptic_clue: Its name means 'Red Uda,' after the river running through it — but before 1934 this city answered to a different name meaning simply 'Upper Uda.'
image_caption: Pedestrian zone on Lenina Street in Ulan-Ude, Russia

name: Vladivostok
peak_smog_season: Winter residential coal and wood heating haze trapped in the harbour basin

analogue_current.note: A comparable monsoon-influenced humid continental Pacific coast climate.

analogue_2050.note: A warmer hot-summer variant of the same coastal East Asian monsoon regime.

urban_fact: For most of the Soviet era, Vladivostok was closed even to foreign visitors, an unusual fate for a naval port founded in 1860 on Golden Horn Bay and laid out in 1868 around a formal, hillside-terraced street grid.
educational_debrief: As the Trans-Siberian Railway's Pacific terminus and home to Russia's Pacific Fleet, Vladivostok stayed a closed military city until 1992, shaping a compact port form distinct from most Siberian sprawl.
cryptic_clue: Its name translates to 'Ruler of the East' — apt for a Pacific naval port sitting closer to Tokyo and Seoul than to its own nation's capital.
image_caption: Waterfront skyline of Vladivostok near Egersheld, Russia

name: Irkutsk
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating temperature-inversion smog trapped in the Angara valley

analogue_current.note: A neighbouring Siberian river city sharing the same severe continental cold-winter regime.

analogue_2050.note: A milder continental climate as extreme winter cold retreats under warming.

urban_fact: A fire in 1879 destroyed much of Irkutsk's original wooden townscape, and what rose in its place was grander: ornate merchant architecture funded by fur-trade and gold-rush wealth that had been accumulating since the city's founding in 1661 on the Angara River, just downstream of Lake Baikal.
educational_debrief: Sitting only 72km from Lake Baikal's outflow, Irkutsk functions as the main gateway to the world's largest freshwater reserve, a proximity that keeps its long-term water outlook unusually secure.
cryptic_clue: Noblemen exiled here after rising against the tsar in 1825 built such elegant wooden mansions that the city earned a nickname borrowed from a much grander European capital.
image_caption: Karl Marx Street in central Irkutsk, Russia

name: Khabarovsk
peak_smog_season: Winter coal-heating haze over the Amur-Ussuri confluence bluffs

analogue_current.note: A neighbouring Manchurian city with the same monsoon-influenced continental rhythm.

analogue_2050.note: A warmer hot-summer continental variant as regional heat intensifies.

urban_fact: Perched on a bluff above the wide Amur floodplain, Khabarovsk's historic core occupies an obviously strategic site: the confluence of the Amur and Ussuri Rivers, where the city was founded in 1858.
educational_debrief: Khabarovsk served as administrative capital of the Russian Far East Federal District from 2002 to 2018, a river-confluence outpost turned regional seat of government.
cryptic_clue: Named for a 17th-century Cossack explorer who never lived to see it built, this bluff-top settlement above two joining rivers sits closer to Tokyo than to its own distant capital.
image_caption: View from Lenin Square down Muravyov-Amursky Street in Khabarovsk, Russia

name: Chita
peak_smog_season: Severe winter coal-smoke inversion trapped in the Transbaikal basin

analogue_current.note: A cross-border steppe-adjacent city sharing the same extreme continental winter cold.

analogue_2050.note: A milder version of the same dry continental steppe climate as winters warm.

urban_fact: Cossacks established Chita in 1653, but the settlement stayed minor for more than two centuries — only once the Trans-Siberian Railway reached it in the 1890s did the city grow into the Transbaikal region's rail and industrial hub.
educational_debrief: Chita once received exiled Decembrist revolutionaries after an 1827 uprising, whose presence helped shape several of the small fortress town’s earliest civic institutions.
cryptic_clue: Aristocratic officers exiled here after an 1825 uprising against the tsar arrived to find little more than a Cossack stockade. Within a century, that stockade grew into capital of a short-lived buffer republic squeezed between a wary Japan and a fledgling revolutionary state to the west, before Moscow folded it back in for good in 1922.
image_caption: Cityscape of Chita, Zabaykalsky Krai, Russia

name: Barnaul
peak_smog_season: Winter heating-season inversion smog over the Ob-Barnaulka confluence

analogue_current.note: Another West Siberian industrial river city on a near-identical continental cycle.

analogue_2050.note: A hotter Central Asian steppe variant of the same continental warming trend.

urban_fact: The Russian Empire's principal silver-processing centre grew up at the confluence of the Ob and Barnaulka Rivers, founded in 1730 by the industrialist Demidov family.
educational_debrief: Barnaul’s identity as a mining-and-metallurgy hub for the mineral-rich Altai Mountains has persisted from imperial silver production well into its modern industrial base.
cryptic_clue: A Ural iron baron shipped two hundred peasants into the Altai foothills in 1730 to build smelting works at a river confluence. Within decades the operation was refining a large share of the empire's silver, a legacy still marked by a stone obelisk commemorating a century of mining in the region.
image_caption: View of Barnaul, Russia from a hill

name: Tomsk
peak_smog_season: Winter heating and petrochemical-industry haze trapped over the Tom River valley

analogue_current.note: A nearby West Siberian city sharing the same wetter, more evenly-distributed continental cycle.

analogue_2050.note: A warmer Urals-region continental climate as summer heat intensifies.

urban_fact: Being bypassed can be a preservationist's blessing: when the Trans-Siberian Railway ran through Novosibirsk instead, Tomsk — founded on the Tom River back in 1604 — missed out on the rapid growth that erased so much historic fabric elsewhere, arguably leaving more of its wooden-lace merchant core intact.
educational_debrief: Home to six universities and Siberia’s oldest, Tomsk State University, the city carries an outsized student population that keeps its demographic profile unusually young for the region.
cryptic_clue: Bypassed by the great trans-continental railway that funneled growth into a rival city instead, this river town's snub left its carved 'wooden lace' merchant houses intact — and its streets, unusually for the region, dense with university students.
image_caption: View of Tomsk, Russia from the fire-observation tower

name: Riyadh
peak_smog_season: Summer Shamal dust storms and photochemical haze over the Najd plateau

analogue_current.note: A near-identical Gulf-interior hot desert climate with the same extreme summer heat.

analogue_2050.note: An even more extreme desert heat regime pushing toward dangerous summer wet-bulb conditions.

urban_fact: Riyadh dismantled its old defensive walls for a 1953 American-influenced grid, later structured by Doxiadis Associates’ 1972 masterplan of 2×2km superblocks along ring roads.
educational_debrief: Riyadh’s decades of ring-road-driven, car-oriented sprawl trace directly back to a single 1972 masterplan grid, one of the more deliberate top-down urban forms in this dataset.
cryptic_clue: A pre-dawn infiltration of a mud-brick fort in January 1902 relaunched a fallen dynasty from this oasis settlement. Seven decades on, a Greek planning firm's superblocks and ring roads squared off the desert capital that raid ultimately built.
image_caption: Riyadh's skyline at night, featuring the Kingdom Centre and Al Faisaliyah Tower

name: Baghdad
peak_smog_season: Spring and summer Shamal sandstorms combined with dry-season vehicle exhaust

analogue_current.note: Another Tigris-basin hot desert city sharing the same extreme summer temperature swing.

analogue_2050.note: An even hotter arid Mesopotamian-basin climate with intensified summer extremes.

urban_fact: Founded in 762 CE as the deliberately circular "Round City," Baghdad’s modern form is bisected by the Tigris into the eastern Risafa and western Karkh districts.
educational_debrief: Baghdad’s founding plan modelled pre-Islamic Sasanian circular cities like Gur, placing the palace and mosque at the exact centre of two concentric defensive walls.
cryptic_clue: A caliph drew a perfect circle of walls around his new capital in 762 CE, seat of a legendary house of learning during the empire's golden age. The ring of walls is long gone, but the great river still splits the city it enclosed into two unequal halves.
image_caption: A view of Baghdad, Iraq from the Medical City building

name: Ankara
peak_smog_season: Winter coal and wood heating inversion trapped on the Anatolian plateau

analogue_current.note: A nearby Anatolian plateau city sharing the same cold semi-arid steppe cycle.

analogue_2050.note: A hotter central Anatolian semi-arid climate with intensified summer heat.

urban_fact: Designated capital in 1923 and planned for 500,000 people, Ankara splits between the historic hilltop citadel quarter of Ulus and the grid-planned republican district of Yenişehir.
educational_debrief: Ankara’s Ulus quarter layers Roman, Byzantine, Seljuk, and Ottoman remains around its citadel, a stark contrast to the deliberately modern grid built for the new republic next door.
cryptic_clue: A breed of long-haired goat still carries this city's old European name into English wool markets, though the young republic that replaced a fallen empire chose, in 1923, to raise its new grid capital beside — not atop — the ancient hilltop citadel already there.
image_caption: View over Ankara at night, with Kocatepe Mosque and Atakule tower visible

name: Amman
peak_smog_season: Spring dust storms and summer photochemical haze over the highland basin

analogue_current.note: A neighbouring Jordanian highland city on the same hot semi-arid seasonal cycle.

analogue_2050.note: A warmer, drier semi-arid Levantine climate with intensified summer heat.

urban_fact: Built across an original seven hills that grew to nineteen, Amman’s Roman-era Citadel and amphitheater overlook a downtown repeatedly reshaped by successive refugee waves since 1948.
educational_debrief: Amman’s modern growth owes less to organic expansion than to repeated forced migration — Palestinian, Iraqi, and Syrian arrivals across seven decades reshaped the capital each time.
